ar.—.. 0 Ult %V EDDINU Title. Cur wedding day, dear John's and mina. At last, at last had come; .... When we as two should cease to lx,, And love and live as one.

How eagerly we talked about The places where we'd go; . All maiden fear was lulled tc , . We loved each other so. The words we said that made us one— We wept our last good-byes; O'er summer seas we sailed and sailed To lands with bluer skies. Where Arno's waters swiftly slip 'Neatli Fonts Vecchio's stones; 'Where Santa Croce's marble saints Watch o'er her honoured bones. ' Where gleam the gems of art divine ds On church and palace walls; Where on the ear the Sistine chant Like seraph music falls. 3 • Across fair Naples' azure bay, Where Capri's smiling. shore • Woos those who love to feast for aye, • Never to wander more. • Through all that land of art and song, Where lova holds sway supreme, We rattmecrand quaffed life's richest draug,n6 • And lived as in a dream. Was this indeed our wedding trip? No., Only what we talked; We went from mother's house to John's, And John and I both walked.

GOLD AND SILVER. Along her father's field they strayed, All decked with cowslips yellow, A little dainty gold-haired maid, A sturdy nine-year fellow. And there love's course they two began, ' (Aix, thorny path for treading!) And vowed when they were maid and man The tbwn should see a wedding. Their golden curls were blown and blent ; Through wafts of fragrance treading; "And oh !" they murmured, well content, "'Twill be a golden wedding !" "'Es time," said he," to claim her vow," And forth he went and found her; ' But she was grown a beauty now, • And half the town was round her. "I see," says he, " yotidon't want me !" Though tears were ripe for shedding,* "I'm glad your eyes are good," says she-- Ah, where's that golden wedding? He dung away, and left her there, , Such heart-sore tear-drops shedding, And gossips cried, in blank despair, "He's spoiled the rarest wedding !" He sailed the seas, be beat the French, ) . • Two-score good years he tarried, And then he thought," That little wenchlr I wonder if she's married ?" Next week a bluff old tar rolled past, The gabled High-street treading, • ! And ancient gossips crowed, "At last • We're like to have the wedding!' ! She'd,waited for him forty years— 1 The grey their locks were threading; And some with smiles, and some with tears, Beheld their silver wedding. —F. LANGBRIDGE, in Good Words.

People whose shoulders are at steady, small, unnoticed wheels are doing that. The mere giving of information, even with the most painstaking explanations, is not enough for mental cul- ture. We must stimulate the mind to -work for itself it its knowledge is to be of any avail. Shallow men believe in their luck, believe:in circum- stances. It was somebody's name, or he happened to be there at the time, or it was so then, and another day it would have been otherwise. Strong men believe in cause and effect.

A youth in the West called George was'eng'aged to be married, but was financially unable to call in the minister. His affianced wanted the affair brought to a finale, but George kept putting her off with promises, saying that he was not able to marry, Sscer Finally, she said, "Dear Gaug, I am willing to marry you if we have to live on bread and water." "Well, well," cried " Gaug," in desperation, "you furnish the bread, and I'll try and skirmish around and hunt up enough water." Conscience is not merely a director for moments of action or decision; it should be a constant guide, urging every man to think rightly as well as to act rightly, and to that end to enlighten his mind, increase his know- ledge, strengthen his judgment, thus fitting him to pur- sue the duties and fill the relations of life with ever- increasing excellence. Some people are accustomed to speak of conscientiousness and intelligence as if they were something separate, but when the true kingdom of conscience becomes established it will be found to em- brace the growth of intelligence as one of its most impor- tant elements. THE TRESPASSER'S LEG.—In the "Traditions of Edin- burgh," we are told that after he had finished his pleasure-grounds, Mr. Ross was much enraged by , affghtly trespassers, and advertised spring-guns and -man-traps without avail. At last he conceived the idea -of procuring a human leg from the Royal Infirmary; sand, dressing it up with a stocking, shoe, and buckle, sent it through the town, borne aloft by the crier, pro- .claiming that "it had been found last night in Mr. Walter Ross's policy at Stockbridge, and offering- to restore it to the disconsolate owner." After this, no one attempted to break into his grounds.—Cassell's "Old and New Edinburgh." A grocer in Kirkcaldy, named Simps6n,"wa's in the habit of taking breakfast in his back shop. - One morn- ing Geordie Dick, the new apprentice, observed that, though the porridge was delivered punctually as usual, his masker showed no signs of retiring to the back shop. Fearin-g the breakfast was getting spoiled. he/looks into j'eont shop, which was crowded with customers, and ' _cre'es, "Meister, yer parritch is come." Mr. Simpson, '"`''eng affronted at .this announcement, took the earliest epportunity of trying to improve Geordie's manners. " Never cry, 'Yer parritch is come,' but say, 'Sir, a gen- tleman is waiting.'" Next morning the 3 same delay occurred, and Geoedie, anxious to show he remembered his lesson, looks in and says, " Sir, a gentlemhn is wait- ing upon you." "All right, George; I'll:be:therein a minute." Ten minutes expired without Mr. Simpson making his appearance. Geordie repeated the announce- ment. "Yes, yes. George; tell the gentleman I'll be just a minute." "Ay, but the gentleman's gettin' aevfu' cauld." Game can be obtained in Paris almost:72,ll the year round by those who know how to ask for it, and this notwithstanding that, the act of buying it out of season is an indictable ofiexce. An attempt was made by the Paris Prefect of 'Nike to put a stop to this practice in a restaurant of great repute. The restaurateur was to be made an example of. A police-agent with the dress and air of a boulevardier entered and asked for pheasant , cooked in a certain manner. No difficulty was raised; the dish was set before him, and he ate it without the slightest scruple. When he had finished, he very quietly and modestly informed the proprietor that he was a police-agent, and that as such he had a painful duty to perform. The restaurateur was equally ciilm and collected. "What IS the matter?" he asked; and, when he was told, he said, with his blandest smile, that the dish of which "monsieur" had just partaken was pre- , Served pheasant. "Then you have some more like it 7" rejoined the other. "No ; you have just eaten the last in stock," was the reply. There was a proces-verbal; but the restaurateur triumphed. A GOOD is a good climate? Where all the organs and tissues of the body are constantly kept at work, alternating with rest. Health is the effect of constant change of all the tissues of the body; change is the essence of that harmony which is health. This har- monyis procured by the constant change in the external agencies supplied to the body through atmosphere and food. A climate which consists in constant moderate variations in its different factors—especially temperature, moisture, light, electricity, wind, and atnsospherie pres- sure—is the best climate for the maintenance and pro- motion of health in fairly vigorous persons. It calls forth the energy of the different organs and functions, their power of adaptation and resistance, and thus keeps them in working condition. Much less good climates are those in which the same conditions prevail for long periods of the year—the same degree of bright sunshine, of:moderate wind, dryness and warmth. In such climates the poWers of adaptation and resistance are not called forth, and are apt to lose their energy: Agreeable climates are not &ways good climates, and disagreeable climates often are the best. The climates of England all the year round are probably the most health-giving in the world. The climates of Italy, of Spain, or Madeira, are infinitely in- ferior. But a climate good for the healthy is ofVn had lot the weak or diseased, whose organs have lost, perman- ently Or temporarily, their power of resistance or adapta- tion, or are partly crippled, So that they cannot come to'the assistance of their allies when these are pressed by inclement elements.—The Hook of Health. Owing to the absence of a member of Mr. Barry Sulli- I van's company while the great tragedian was stamne in the provinces, the prompter's services were brought into requisition. Be had never been on the stage before, but did very well until the third act, where ,there was a dis- tinct pause, and, forgetting the situation, he began giv- ing the cue. He gave it several times, looking anxiously at every actor on the stage. The audience here began to titter, erhen Sullivan said to him,in a savage whispisr, "Why don't you go on, you idiot? It's your cue." He had been prompting himself. In one of the many picturesque little hamlets which stud the banks of the river Ayr, one of her Majesty's Inspectors was having his annual inspection of the parish school. He was examining a class on Scottish history, and, wishing to elicit the historical fact of James the Fifth's quarrel with his Queen, Mary of Lorraine, asked the question, "Why was Mary Queen of Scots born at Linlithgow?" when up starts a bright little fellow and shouts, "Because her mither was there." "Well," re- plied the Inspector," there might have been some doubt as to the aLswer I would have given, but there cal be 1 none about yotire'," Some time ago a Sloop *as loading potatoes; at MAW, gordon. A cart from the country came alongside of her, and the driver proceeded to empty his load into the vessel's hold. When he was finished, he was accosted by the mate, and invited to warm and dry himself by the galley fire, for the morning was wet and stormy, and he had a good many miles to go ere he reached home. Alter a while the mate gave the man a ship's biscuit and a piece of salt beef,- the former as hard as a flint. The driver ate the beef heartily, without touching the biscuit. When he had finished, he handed back the in- digestible biscuit to the mate, with the remark—" Here, sailor man, there's yer plate." A short time after the present Bishop of Worcester had been appointed to that see, he had occasion to travel through Banbury by rail. Being desirous to test, and at the same time encourage, the far-famed industry of the town, and as the train stopped for a short time in the station, he beckoned to a boy and inquired the price of the celebrated cakes. "Threepence each, sir," said the boy. Handing him sixpence, the bishop desired him to s bring one to the carriage, adding, "And with the other threepence buy one for yourself." The boy shortly re- turned, complacently munching his Banbury, and handing threepence Lin coppers to the bishop; exclaimed, "There' was only one left, guy'nor !" STRIVE FOR A GOOD NASEE.—Although riches, learning, and high position are within the reach only of a few, a good character may be obtained by every person; and a good name is better than all these. It is important to every individual. It is necessary in aff situations. It becomes the source of. the purest gratifications. It is the most solid honorer. If we are without it, we can gain no sincere respect among our feirow creedures. Should respect be paid to a person destitute of character, it is only on account of extrinsic circumstances which . compel the tongue to use language that the feefings of the heart condemn. Without a character which com- mands respect, our importence in society is unfelt, and the bloom and vigour of life pass without a proportion- ate elevation in the commumty ef which we forma pare. According as we are deficient in character we sink in public estimation. SponeVloseer.—For several centuries past, and until comparatively recent times, persons wearing' spurs in any sacred edifice in England were accosted either by choristers or beadles, who demanded a fee, by way of fine, for thus entering a cathedral. minsterror church,. and thereby interrupting the service. Two er three centuries ago, when spurs were- commonly wern;, the- amount received for "spur-money" was considerable; and singing-boys and beadles were ever on the alert for- the ringing of the spurred boot„eften to the neelect of their more legitimate duties. Sometimes the choristers lost their perquisite because of their inability to repeat the gamut on the demand of spur-weafing. persons. From the cheque-book of the Chapelenyee,. Dr. Rimbault made the following extract of ' an order made by the Dean in 1.622 :—" That if anie knight or ether persone entituled to weare spurs enter the Chappell in that guise, he shall pay to the euiristers the acenstonsedl fine; but if he command the youngest quirister to repeats his gamut, and lie fade in the so doing ,the said knight, or other. shall not pay the fine." °This rule- was enforced until about the year 1830. Quoting &note in Gifford's edition of the work of Ben Jenson, Mr: . Markland says: "In the time of Ben -Jenson, in conse- quence of the interruptions to divine service occasioned' by the ringing of the spurs worn by persons- walking and transacting business in cathedrals, and especially in. St. Paul's, a small fine was imposed on them; called ' spursmoney,' the exaction of which was committed to. the beadles and singing-boys." Under the title of "The- Children of the Chapel stript and whipt," there- was published a curious tract, in which the . following passage, bearing upon the subject of spuremoneye occurs: "Wee think it very necessarye that every quorister shoulde bringe with him to church a Testa- ment in Englishe, and turne to everie chapter as- it ie. daily read, or some other goad and godly Prayer-book; ' rather than spend their tyme in talk and hunting after- ' spur-money, wherein they set their whole miverese and' ' doe often abuse dyvers if they doe not bestows some- what on them." Spur-money was, exacted in Westmin- ster Abbey from Dr. Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, who handed over an eighteenpenny token as the fine. The penalty was also imposed, about the same time, on. the Duke of Cumberland (afterwards King of Hanover). for entering the choir of the same abbey in his spurs; but his Royal Highness, who was installed there., excused himself with great readiness, pleading his right to wear his spurs in that church, inasmuch as it wee the- place where they were first put on him. About 1847 or 1848 a party of sappers and miners were stationed at Peterborough, engaged in the trigonometrical survey, when the officer entered the cathedral with his spurs on, and was immediately beset by the choristers, who de- manded money of him for treading the sacred flbor with armed heels. One of the dignitaries was ignorant of the practice.—Chembers's Joareal. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were preeent the It9v. Gt, IF. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. rshickhutat, Jolley, Greening, Gibson, W, Houghton, J. Houghton, Isherwood, Darbyshire, Brown, Clark, Ratcliffe, Wright, Jones, Swinton, Harrison, Voisey. Ba'harry, gilstisll, Strange, Pennington, Heaton, J. C. Sutton (cleric), and S. Sutton (asAstant clerk.) Mr. Henley, one of the inspectors of the Local Gcvernment Board was also present. SCHOOL FEES.

The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in„180 cases, 147 of which were renewals, and 33 new cases —Mr. Snows, moved the adoption of the minutes. —Mr. JOLLEY. in seconchne„ was sorry to say that owing to badness of trade many of these cases had to be granted for 13 weeks. Many of the people were just on the verge of pauperism. (Mr. HARRISON: Starvation.) One woman who came before them said she bad not a bite of food in the house for her children. The poverty in these cases was not due to drunkenness or idleness, but want of work.—The CHAIRMAN said he often thought there was as much dis- tress above the line of pauperism as below it.

div.head: SCHOOL COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL COMMITTEE.

In the minutes of the Industrial Schools Committee it was stated that the beperintendent had repotted the general health of the children to be excellent. The committee had informed Mr. and Miss Gibbon that they bad concluded to terminate their engagement as father and mother of No. 1 I home, a month's notice being allowed.—The CHAIRMAN •moved the adoption of the minutes, and Mr. JOLLEY having seconded, this less agreed te. In his journal the Snrwin- tendent reported that the children bad been invited by Mr. Sheridan Pa witness a performance of '6 Grelloy's Money" at the Theatre Royal, WarriNton, and this they had dune , and enjoyed, it very much.

All the inhabitants who had time to take refuge did so; but Shefket had a couple of mountain guns (4-pounders), and after a shot or two broke open the doors. At this time I suppose that there were not mose than 50 surviving families, all established in huts on the ruins of their former homes. That they were saved from suffering what their fathers and mothers, their sons and their daughters had suf- fered was due to the initiative of Idris Bey, when he hit upon the idea of sending out a Mixed Commission. Many Mussulmans, as honest as he was but without his pluck, would have sent " irregulars " to explore; and then what would have happened? • Next morning we. rode to Yamboli, and found the town full of Circassian "irregulars:" most of whom saluted me with the• ordinary. " Welcome, , " (" Khosh. gueldin, Effendim "). We went straight `to the Kaimakam's (sort of prefect's) residence. and there I told him my opinion of his lying telegram about rebels being mustered at iloyadjik: 10 colleagues, even the archbishop, would not begin to tell him our views of his conduct; but even their timidity did not prevent them chiming in when I used some of the most impolite Turkish epithets -that ever made use of to a Turkish official. Whilst we were at Government House news came to the Kaitnakam that two villages—one Christian *mad one Turkish—were blockaded by Circassians who [had carried tiff all the cattle and sheep. He ordered out a battalion (2,50) of the Mustahafyz—the Lanckturm or Arriere Ban of the 'Turkish army. These poor fellows were armed with lower percussion muskets C!' G. 13," 1832), and they did't care much to go and face the Cit- cassian horsemen. Shortly afterwards we learned that the Circasstans would not give up the flocks and herds they , had taken; but they would not lire on the ' Sultan's troops unless Provoked. The result was that the Circassians carried everything off, and the Landshirm aetired. After this, and . before we left the town' the Circassians constantly answered me? " Steal ? not at all 'you don't understand. We have our orders." And, as I knew later, they had orders to carry off everything in the way of commis- sariat that might be useful to the advancing Russian troops. Ile next day (I had forgotten to say that we posted four gendarme at Boyadjik) we returned to Sliven, with the pleasing consciousness that we had saved Boyadjik from a second massacre.

A VILLAGE IN DANGER. One gvening, about 11 o'clock, a policeman came to the house where I was staying at Sliven,,and asked, with the governor's compliments, whether I would be good enough to come down to see him, as he had some serious business on hand. This govertior was such a good fellow so honest and so plucky—that I was bound to go and hear 'what he had to say. He received me in his bed- room (the Turkish gentleman's bed is generally a plank sofa covered with rugs), and, after the salutation, said: "You know the village of /3oyadjik ?" "Yes, by name." "Well, look, here ; telegram from Crevemr-general Of Adrianople says Kaimakam of Yamboll reports 20 armed Bulgar rebels in that village; orders me to make inquiry, and to send troops, if necessary, to quell in- surrection." ("Troops," when there are no regulars to be had, is interpreted as" Bashi-bazouks.") I asked Idris Effendi what he meant to do, and why he wanted me. "1 am going to send a Mixed Com- mission—Mussul mans and B ulgars—to find out the rights of this affair, because I believe it's all a lie; and I want you to let your kavass go with them, to report to you and see whether there are 'or are not rebels in that village." Nearly all day I had been riding through the deserted villages, passing miles and miles of land where the harvested sheaves awaited only the carts that were never to coin; and. I was very tired and wished to go to bed. But, knowing Idris Effendi, I suggested that he perhaps really meant to ask me to go with the commission; and then he allowed that he hoped I might volunteer, as he could scarcely trust Turks or Bulgars. So it was settled; 5 a.m. to start. Commission His Beatitude Seraphim, Archbishop of Sliven. 2. Michelaki Bey (Bey, though a Bulgat, because he had the Order of the Medjidieh). 3. Kieur Artin Effendi, a Christian Armenian. 4. Yangueus Aarif Effendi, my acl- litus when I was governor of Sliven. 5. Tchilli Osman Aga, a Turkish member of the Mutessarif's Council. 6. Amoudjah Bey. Twelve mounted police (sonvari zaptich) were to be put absolutely under my orders, and the whole commission was, more or less, to act on my ad- vice. This meant, of course, that if anything went wrong it would be my fault; but I had already taken so much serious responsibility that a little more or less seemed but a trifle.

I dare say that some people will recollect that the village of Boyadik was "taken" in the year of the Bul- gariar insurrrection, by Shefket Pasha with one or two mountain-guns,regular troops, and Bashi-barouks. The fighting was all on one side. Over 200 Balgara were killed (me Bulgar fired a shot), but one poor Tartar pashi-basouk was most unfortunately killed.. This un- lucky folksy', wearing his own sheepskin cap, went into a deserted 'Bulgarian cottage, where he changed his own clothes for new Bulgarian breeches and jacket. Coming out at the cbor,two Turks fired at hinr; and as he fell he cried out, *Brothers in the faith, what have you done? lam a Alussulman !" Then the two Turks ran up and, legging his pardon, said it was "all a mis- take.' But,, said they, "this poor brother in the Faith (Dian, Kardasodi) can't live, and he suffers terribly; let ra cut his head off." They did so; and I really believe they thought they had done a charitable act. I wonder whether killing wounded men can be excused by these races on the ground of humanity ? I know that Servians and Bulgarians in their war of last year gave. such n reason. for despatching the wouaded; but I fear that a good warm capote was sometimes a great temptation to half-starved, half-frozen, and half- dreesed soldiers. _

UNITED STATES AND CANADA. Gnaw*, bI:INDAY.—The new Franchise Act having come into operation, the Governor-General, on the advice of the Cabinet, yesterday dissolved Parliament, in order to bring the Dominion House of Commons into accord with the en- larged electorate. Tbe United states Convress has passed a bill with the L avowed object of extirpating Mormonism. It is thought I (says a despach from Washington) to be a grave question I whether, under this provision Congress has the right to dissolve a religous corporation because its members break the Irma. Sate FRAWCISCO, SUNDAS.—A derelict schooner with a catgo of giant powder exploded off Golden Gate to-day. Several passengers were injured, and the Cliff House Hotel ond other buildings were ruined. THE CANADIAN ,FISHERIES QUESTION. WASHINGTON. WEDNESDAY.—The Foreign Affairs Corn- enittee of the House of Representatives has issued its repent on the Canadiantaheriee question. The Committee recoua- anends that so long as American fishing vessels in Canadian [waters are excluded from touching or trading at Dominion harbours, a similar course should he observed in American ports with regard to Canadian vessels..

MEMORIAL SERVICE AT WESTMINSTER ABBEY.

Concurrently with the funeral ceremony at Upton Pynes churchyard, yesterday afternoon, a solemn service was held at Westminster Abbey, as a last mark of respect to ,the deceased Earl of Iddesleigh, by his late colleagues in the Government and his associates and friends in political and private life. Seldom has a more touching or im- pressive tribute been paid to a deceased statesman than that which the scene at the Abbey conveyed. All who were celebrated in public life in the country were present, or represented in one shape or form, at the gathering, and the remarkable scene was witnessed by a concourse, the deraear our of which was that of 'a family attending the obsequies of a near relative rather than those of a states- man who may to most of them have been peisonally un- familiar. The modest decorations of crape on the choir stalls which formed the only mourning paraphernalia in the Abbey were heightened by the sombre dress of the con- gregation. Royalty, ministers, peers, commoners, am- bassadors, Government officials, and the greater, but un- distinguished, throng which filled the unappro- priated spaces, were all attired in sober black, few men being without a band of crape on the hat or the arm. The great congregation were assembled long before three o'clock, the hour fixed for the service, arriving silently and without ostentation in groups of two or three, or more, and all being seated at the time when the mournful cortege must have been starting .from the Pynes for the Earl's last resting place. When at last the occupiers of priviledged places in the choir, and the space beneath the lantern, had filled their allotted seats, many well-remembered faces were to be seen. On the north side of the choir were assembled, in the knights' stalls, most of the members of the Ministry —Lord Salisbury, Mr. W. H. Smith, Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Mr. Stanhope, Lord George Hamilton, Lord John Manners, Lord Cross, Lord Cmnbrook, the Lord Chancellor, Lord Stanley of Preston. and Sir Henry Holland. Mr. Arthur Balfour and Mr. Henry Matthews had seats on the opposite side of the chancel, near the Lord Chancellor (Baron Herschell). The re- maining Cabinet Minister, Mr. Goschen, was absent in Liverpool on election business, and another member or the Government, Mr. C. T. Ritchie, was absent in scot: land. Other occupants of the choir were the Duke of Cambridge, Prince Henry of Battenberg (representing the Queen), Col. the Hon. W. J. Colville (representing the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh), and Sir H. Elphin- stone (representing the Duke of Connaught), while among the assembly were many representatives of foreign Powers, and prominent statesmen and poli- ticians of all shades, including Mr. Mundella, Lord Cranborne, Mr. Stuart Wortley, Mr. Childers, Mr. Henry Manners (private secretary to Lord Salisbury), Lord Rowton. the Lord Mayor of London, Viscount Wey- mouth, Mr. Philip Currie, Sir John Gorst, the Rocorcler of Exeter, Lord Walter Gordon-Lennox, Sir Walter Phillimore, the Hon. Rae Barrington (private secretary to thca late Lord Iddesleigh), Mr. Guy Dawnay, Viscountess Sidmouth, and Sir A. West. The service was opened by the recital of the first part of the burial service by the choir, in procession from the nave to the choir, followed by the Dean, assisted by Canon Rowsell and Archdeacon Farrar, all the congregation standing in deep and re- spectful silence. Then the choir chanted the Psalms 39 ..nd 90. and the special lesson was read. The Nu=

Dintittis was then sung, and at this time a cense DlaCK- ness suddenly overspread the church like a pall and shrouded the whole building in a funeral gloom befitting the occasion. This continued during the remainder of the service.

The Prime Minister followed the service from a large. Prayer Book with earnest attention, his tall and bowed figure bending closely over the pages, while the solemn Liturgy was 'being read or sung, and only when the strains of Spohr's beautiful anthem "Blest are •Ihe departed" were stirring the hearts of those present by their mournful cadences was Lord Salisbury seen to look up, and he was then observed to be greatly affected, and. unable to restrain one or two large tears which appeared on his cheek. Others of the late Earl's former colleagues ! were seen to be similarly affected as the pure harmony , of the boys' voices swelled out, and amongst them Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Mr. W. H. Smith, Lord Cranbrook, and Lord Jolan Manners, all close friends of the dead states- man, were deeply moved. The closing prayers of the burial service were then read, and the hymn, "Now the labourer's task is o'er," concluded the service. Then amid the solemn pulsations of the "Dead March from Saul" the congregation silently dispersed, the royalties leading the way, followed by the ministers and the general body of the assemblage. each of the more distinguished shaking hands with Dean Bradley, as he passed out through the Jerusalem Chamber.

div.head: MEMORIAL SERVICE AT. EDINBURGH CATHEDRAL.
div.p: MEMORIAL SERVICE AT. EDINBURGH CATHEDRAL.

A funeral service was held at St. Giles's Cathedral, Edinburgh, Lord Iddesle,igh being Lord Rector of the University of Edinburgh. There was a large congrega- tion, including a great number of graduates and stu- dents, the Chancellor of the University, the principal, and other officials, as well as the profess= in their robes. The Rev. Dr. Cameron Lees preached, and delivered au impressive eulogitun onthe deceased Lord Rector. In nearly all the towns of Devonshire, and in many other parts of the kingdom, there were public demonstra- tions of mourning during the time the funeral was taking place.

div.head: RECEI)TION AT THE COLONIAL OFFICE.
div.p: RECEI)TION AT THE COLONIAL OFFICE.

Sir Henry Holland, upon his appointment to the Colonial Secretaryship, on Monday afternoon officially received the Agents-General of the Colonies in his pri- vate room at the Colonial Office. There were present the Agents-General of South Australia, Sir A. Blyth ; New Zealand, Sir F. D. Bell; and Cape Colony, Sir Charles Mills. Sir A. Blyth introduced the agents in the absence of Sir Charles Tupper, the High Corn- missioner for Canada, 'who sailed on Sunday for the Dominion. Sir J. Berry and Sir Saul Samuel were also unavoidably absent. Sir Arthur Blyth, in introducing the colonial representatives, congratulated Sir Henry Holland upon his appointment, and said that in paying the respects of the colonies through their agents, they simply asked him, as they had asked his predecessors in office, that he should place as favourable a construction as possible upon any communication they might make to him in connection with the colonies they respectively represented.—Sir Hy. Holland, in reply, acknowledged with great satisfaction 'their kind address and the manner in which they received his Uppointment. He could confidently promise to carry out the desire expressed on their part in regard to the consideration of colonial matters. It was true that he had had some previous experience of the Colonial Office, but if that previous connection should in any degree tend to lighten his labours, it brought with it at the same time a higher sense of the difficulties and respon- sibilities of the post, and therefore a greater appreciation of the advantage of receiving information from the re- presentatives of the colonies, and allowing their views to have due weight with him upon all questions of Importance. One alteration he had noticed since he was a permanent official at the Colonial Office, wastle in- creased importance now attached to the office of agents- general. He regarded this as a step in:the right direc- tion, and he hoped to obtain from them special assist- ance upon various important matters. It appeared to him that this year of the Queen's Jubilee would be ap- propriately marked by.the proposed conference of repre- sentatives of the Great Colonies, and felt that the dis- cussion which would doubtless take place was likely to tend to the result desired by all, a closer union of the colonies with the mother country. Sir Henry Holland then shook hands with the agents-general, and again naaedhig thanks for their kind congratulations.
LECTURE ON NOXIOUS VAPOURS. BLACK SMOKE IN WARRINGTON.

In connection with the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society a lecture free to the public was given in the lecture room at the Museum, on 1 Tuesday evening, on "Noxious vapours which pollute i the air," by Mr. J. Carter Bell, the well-known pub- lic analyst. There was a large attendance,although ' the weather was inclement, and there were two or three other attractions in the town the same evert- ing. In the absence of the president (Mr. T. G. Rylands) Alderman Burgess presided. Prior to the commencement of the lecture, Mr. H. F. Greenhough, chemist, Warrington, and Mr. John Coxon, tanner, Latchford, were accepted as mem- bers of the society, and it was announced by Mr. J. R. Young, that the lecture proposed to be given by Mr. Worsley would positively be given in a fort- night from that day. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Circumstance@ over which they had no control had compelled them to postpone it once or twice. Mr. J. CARTER BELL introduced his .lecture by quoting/the words of the poet, "Comes a vapour from the,margin, blackening over heath and bolt," which were, he said, unfortunately too true in this district, for they had only to go to the outskirts of their cities and towns to find heaths, fields, pas- tures, and gardens which in years gone by were the delight of those whose lot it was to dwell in their midst, that had been literally "watered with the dews of hell." The result was that the heath was , no longer gay with its liveried yellow, nor were the 1 fields covered with green grass, nor did the trees in , the gardens " bend down with weight of fruit to I I kiss their mother earth." In the place of that ' joyous scene, they had trees stretching their gaunt 1 and withered arms, and pointing to the authors of the scene of destruction who had made the treeless pastures, with the Stygian streams meandering through, upon whose banks were unctuous slime and stonied weariness, a very picture of desolation. And the cause of all this weary waste was due to certain noxious vapours, which carried death in their hideous folds and "as they kissed consumed." 1 These were belched forth from chimneys far and I wide, till the landscape was one veritable Gehenna. 1 The chief vapours he would speak about were hy- drochloric acid, chlorine, sulphurous acid, nitric acid, sulphuretted hydrogen, and arsenical vapours. Hydrochloric acid was very largely produced when common table salt was decomposed by sulphuric acid or oil of vitriol. That was the first stage in the manufacture of washing soda. Common salt was thrown into a furnace, and a certain amount of oil of vitriol was poured upon the salt. Imme- diately dense acid vapours were evolved, which were most destructive to all vegetation and works of art. Anyone could see for himself the effects of the gas upon flowers and green leaves, for he need, only place about half an ounce of common salt in a tumbler, and pour upon the salt about the same weight of oil of vitriol, when dense fumes would be immediately given off; and if a bunch of flowers or green leaves were suspended in the gitethe betatity of the flowers and leaves would soon depart. The lecturer then referred to the effects of this as on Halstead Park, an estate about five or six miles from Widnes. The trees on some parts of the es- tate were nearly all destroyed, and the bark from the dead oak trees was rendered valueless by the action of the acid vapours. The growth of grass was sliddenly arrested by the passage of these va- pours over it, and even the hay was spoiled and ac- ted injuriously on the cattle. As an illustration of the evil effects of this gas upon cattle, a farmer, living about a mile from Widnes, had 50 cows, and sometimes he had to kill 10 or 12 a year, owing to their health being seriously impaired. He had visi- ted Runcorn and the neighbourhood, and could speak of the vast amount of damage that has been done to the district. Gardens, fruit trees, hedges, gorse, and bramble all disappear under the influence of this deadly gas, and the only plants which maintained the struggle for existence were the common elder and the deadly nightshade. Mr. Bell afterwards referred to the black smoke nuis- ance, and remarked that he should think there was plenty of work for the smoke nuisance inspector in Warrington. This smoke contained a large quantity of sulphureous acid which passed into their atmosphere. But they also got this acid from the gas in their houses and it was the cause of the destruction of so many books in libraries. (Hear, hear.) It did seem a pity that with all their vast amount of science they were not able to give the inhabitants of towns a , purer atmosphere than that they were living under; but science was still advancing, and it might be , that the time will come when all these vapours would be done away with, when they should be living under clear blue skies, and not under the fogs they had lately been having. (Applause.) This was due to a great extent, to his mind, to the way works were carried on. because in Cornwall. where coals were. dear there was little smoke emptied from the chimneys, and he had been told by some one that he could scarcely tell by looking at the chimneys whether the works were being car- ried on or not. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The lecture was enlivened and illustrated by numerous experiments, and proved to be extremely interest- ing,

The CHAIRMAN said there was a fact which none of them should be ignorant of, and that was that while they had a smoke inspector in Warrington who was discharging his duties as well as an in- spector could—in fact, there were three inspectors at work—there was no town of the same dimen- sions and with the same number of inhabitants that had the same volume of dense black smoke per- petually flowing over it. The fact was that the lesser offenders were brought up and punished, and the great ones escaped scot-free. That was no fault of the authorities and the inspectors. He did not know it was anyone's fault, in fact; but an Act was passed in 1875 known as the Public Health Act, which fortified and protected the large producer of smoke in Warrington against all action that might jbe brought against him by any authority, and henee they had an enormous quantity of dense black smoke poured out in 'Warrington, he would not say to its prejudice—that was for chemists to say—but that it was exceedingly inconvenient he did know. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. ROBERT DAVIES proposed a vote of than to the lepturer, and remarked that there was another side to the quesuion to that which had been presented to themthat night. All Warringtonians would agree that the very saddest sights that could ever meet their eyes in coming into Warringtan would be to find that none of the numerous chim- neys were emitting black smoke. (Applause.) The reason the Legislature did not apply the Acts to ironworks was, he had always understood, because there was no process known to science which could enable the manufacturer of iron to produce his ma- terial without turning out black smoke very much as it was in Warrington. At the same time it was a very great pity indeed that these operations could not be carried on without injuring vegetation, and without making the air they breathed, as the lecturer had said, more or less a nuisance to them. (Applause.) Mr. THOMAS Mounts seconded the vote of thanks. The first part of the lecture, he said, was very nice indoed—(laughter)--but whilst these confounded gases were being given off, the most useful products in arts and sciences were being produced, and which they could not without in these days of cultiva- tion. They mur have them, nuisance or no nuis- ance, With regard to smoke and economy Mr. Mor- ris remarked that if there was a place where coal ought to be economized it was on winerchant vessa out at sea; but let them go on a steamer from Dublin to Holyhead, and they would find there was one vast volume of smoke 'given out of the funnel. Ask the man why he produced it, and he would re- ply, "if I don't I get no steam, and the vessel won't go." (Applause.) He challenged his friend Dr. Carter Bell that if he would give him a wrinkle in making iron without producing smoke he would pay him well. (Laughter and aol.lause.) Mr. Morixs supported the vote of thanks, and said manufacturers had sufficient interest in trying 1 to consume smoke. They might yet seeiron manu- factured in Warrington without smoke, especially f the petroleum wells near the Caspian gave out the quantity of oil they were said to do, and if that oil could be brought to Warrington to be used in manufacturing iron instead of coal. (Hear, hear.) At present ironworkers had to face a practical diffi- culty. They had to make profits as well as smoke, and they preferred profit and smoke to no smoke and no profits. (Laughter and applause.) Councillor DIXON and Dr. HURTER, of Widnes, also supported the vote of thanks which was then heartily accorded, and having been acknowledged by Mr. Bell the proceedings closed.

INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARr • BALL. The annual ball in aid of the funds of the War- rington Infirmary and Dispensary was held in the Assembly-room at the Lion Hotel, on Tuesday even- ing, and was a great success. Nearly 150 people were present, dancing, whin commenced at nine o'clock, being continued until nearly two o'clock on Wednesday morning. The ball-room had for the occasion been elaborately decorated, the work having : been entrusted to Mrs. O'Brien, and the manageress • of the hotel, Miss Hart, supplied an excellent sup- - per. THE AMERICAN MAlLS.—Tenders for carrying the Trans. atlantic mails from March let have been received, but will not be decided until Parliament has had an opportunity of discussing the whole question. ALBERT HOLSWORTR, who was engaged as banksrnan at the Houghton Main Collery when the accident involving the , loss of ten lives occurred on December 30th, has been arres- ted on a charge of manslaughter. The death of. one of the workmen at the Talacre Mine, , Meliden. near Rhyl, through a fall down the shaft, which he met with when descending by means of a ladder, has led to a coroner's jury returning a verdict of manslafighter against a "syndicate" of seven gentlemen who have been working the mine for about six weeks. DELIBERATE WIFE MURDER—The Grimsby magistrates on Monday cornrnittPd for trial at Lincoln Assizes a fisher. ' man. named Richard Insole, aged 24. who was charged with having murdered his wife. On the 7th inst. the winner, who had not lived happily with his wife, bought a revolver, and, going to the hduse where the unfortunate woman waa staying, fired at her several times, inflicting wounds which proved fatal. He then tried to stab himself, but did no serion. harm.

And yet the rate- endeavour to " take it all in ; " but the result payers are asked to believe that the change is is a bad fit of indigestion, and the last state being made in their interests I Out upon of that man is worse than the first. Tnere is such trash ; it is the veriest cant, and the therefore a wide field for the Liberal League, ratepayers ought to deal with it by holding an and we would advise those who wish to labour indignation meeting, and making a strong ap- in it to lose no time in putting themselves in peal to the Education Department not to communication with the General Secretary, sanction the proposed change. 'at his offices, 18, Cockspur-street, Pall Mall, Dean FINEGAN urged that the increase London, for he is willing., nay eager, to be of would not affect the poor people, as the Board service in forming lodges of the Liberal had machinery in force to pay their fees." League. What machinery—the machinery of the In- I quisition ? Are parents who are pinching, " TOUCH AND GO." themselves to keep three or four children at I , There has been quite a series of accidents school to be told that, if they feel the pres- 1 at St. Helens ; two children burned to sure of the 50 per cent increase, they must to death ; on marl killed a'a a glassworks, torture themselves by laying bare their poverty and another at a colliery. "One woe doth before a Committee of Inquiry, and pauperise tread upon another's heel, so fast they fol- themselves by having the fee paid out of the bow " rates? Rather than do this many of them will either take their children away altogether when they reach the higher standards, or send them to the lower tee denominational schools; and perhaps this is what Dean FINE- GAN would like to see. The Rev. G BOND said " many people objected to educating other people's children up to so high a stan- dard :" and we can quite believe it. They are of the narrow-souled clerical older, who do not believe in freedom, either in mind or body. except for themselves. They are of the class who supported the slaveholders of America when the punishment was death for teaching a slave to read ; who opposed the extension of the franchise in England, and who stand to-day in the way of Free Education. But what does the Rev. G. BOND mean by " educating other people's children ?" If these " other people" pay their rates and send their children to school with the fee in their hand, they are surely not much indebted to him. He ought to know, and he has no busi- ness on the School Board if he does not know, that "educating other people's chil- dren "—even when the parents are poor or too improvident to pay anything--is a good thing in itself; that it greatly reduces juve- nile crime ; that it finds less work for policeman, judge, and jailer ; and conse- quently that money spent in this way is an investment of the best kind. As Mr. Timm's, the chairman of the Board, forcibly remarked, "it was a loss to them as a Corn- munity, and a loss to us as a nation to let children go away imperfectly educated." But the three clerics on the Widnes School Board are not moved by considerations of this kind. They show, at any rate, more re- gard for the denominational schools with which they are ccnnected than they do for Board Schools. They represent their de- nominations—they do not represent the rate- payers, and the sooner the ratepayers realise this, and act accordingly, the better it will be for their interests.

Newton Improvement Commissioners are I very kind. The police prosecuted a man for falsely pretending that he was a toll col- lector, and he was sent to gaol for three months. The costs of the prosecution amounted to £9 35 4d, and the Commis- sioners—altlaough they pay rates and taxes— have paid the bill. They grumbled, but still I they paid. It is very kind of them, and they cannot be surprised if they are asked to pay other bills for police prosecutions.

, - Whilst the clergy on the Widnes School Board have voted for a reduction of school teachers' salaries, the "Reverend sirs" of the Prescot Rural Deanery have declared in favour of " a diocesan jubilee memorial for the purpose of augmenting the stipends of the clergy. There is certainly a great gulph between the pay of a curate at 2roo a year, and that of an archbishop at £lO,OOO. One archbishop may be of more value than many sparrows; but it is coming it rather too strong to say, as the salary seems to say, that he is worth just as much as roo curates.

With regard to the proposed Church House, the Rev. Dr. Cameron spoke out pretty plainly. He does not want to have anything to do with "a white elephant," a jimcrack palace, or "a gigantic job with an architect at the bottom of it." Dr. Cameron is not a bishop, and he does not understand how bishops feel. They certainly might be content to hum- bly follow Him who had not where to lay His head; and they do, but they are a very long way behind when they ask for a Church House at the cost of Two Hundred Thousand Pounds.

Friends of Free Education will have to keep their armour bright; the conflict is not far distant. The reactionaries on the Widnes School Board have already more than once shown their hand. They have been raising the school fees, and reducing the salaries of the teachers, and exbect by this process to make the schools more Successful ! It is rather the way to ruin them. The anti-Board School members would like denominational schools to be supported out of the rates; but they want this without paying the proper price—that is, letting the ratepayers' repre- sentatives have control of the schools.

THE Liberal League which is being formed to checkmake the operations of the Primrose League is making progress. Its object is to "band together men and women in .every part of the Empire, and of all grades of so- ciety, for the promotion of Liberal prin- ciples." There is nothing fanciful in this ; it is work that requires doing; and, since women are in some cases being brought into action in a pernicious way in connection with the Primrose League, it is extremely desir- able that the fair sex on the Liberal side should have the opportunity of doing what they can to lessen the mischief. Of course, to be consistent, those who advocate a Liberal League of this kind should be pre- pared, or be preparing themselves, for an ex- tension of the Parliamentary franchise to women ; and, as we are amongst those who think this should be done, seeing that they possess the franchise in matters Municipal, we hope the new League will live and thrive. It has one advantage over the Primrose League, and that is in name; its title is not ridiculous in itself, nor does it make any statesman, living or .dead, look ridiculous. Lord BEACONSFIELD is said to have been an admirer of the primrose ; but what if he had been fond of pickled cabbage? Would it have been equally flattering to him to have had a Pickled Cabbage League? If there is one thing more than another that Lord BEACONSFIELD would' have been dis- posed to sneer at, it would have been the attempt, if it had been made whilst he was alive, to have a statesman held in rememembrance, not by his labours for the State, but by the particular flower which he happened to favour. It is the sort of thing which might be appropriate for the "Miss Nancy" of politicians, but to associate it with a sturdy leader of men, like the late Earl, is to inflict an injury alike on the flower and the peer. The appellation Liberal League is therefore better than that of Primrose League. In a circular we have received, the , Secretary, Mr. J. DRAKE DIGBY, says :—" The strong common sense of Liberals and Radi- cals revolts from the fanciful titles of Knights, Dames, and Associates, and all the members of this League are to be known by the simple term of Companion.'" We quite agree as to the absurdity in such a connection of the titles of Knight and Dame, and we suspect that" Primrosers " themselves feel that they sit awkwardly upon them, for these empty but high-sounding adjuncts do not figure very prominently in reports of their proceedings. But what of "Companion" which is to be applied to those who are connected with the Liberal League? We must, to be frank, say that seems only just a little less ridiculous than "Knight" or "Dame." We have "Com- panions of the Bath," "Companions of St. Michael and St. George," &c., and now we are to have "Companions of the Liberal League." Why be tarred, in however small a way, with this brush ? " The strong com- mon sense of Liberals and Radicals revolts" from it, and would much prefer the simple and intelligible phrase—" members of the Liberal League." With this exception, we must say that the new League is being estab- lished on sound lines. and that, if lodges are organised throughout the country, it is ex- ceedingly likely that good work will be ac- complished. A great change, fortunately, has come over the education question since Sir William Berkeley, the aristocratic Governor of Vir- ginia, wrote :---" I thank God there are no free schools or printing, and I hope we shall not have them these hundred years. For learning has brought heresy and disobedi- ence and sects into the world, and printing has divulged them, and libels against the best government. God keep us from both."

The "best government" in Sir William's days was English tyranny over the American colonists; but education did its work—all that was swept away when George the Third was King; and now America is the land of Free Schools. In "Triumphant Demo- cracy," Mr. Carnegie, says : " For every pound spent by Great Britain for the educa- tion of her people, more than four pounds are squandered upon the Army and Navy. The Republic reverses this practice, and spends nearly two pounds upon education for every one pound spent in war." Carlyle might well say that the people inhabiting these islands were some thirty millions- mostly fools.

The Wesleyan Young Men and Young Women's Bible Class at Earlestown have been favoured by having an interesting paper read to them by a young lady, on the subject of Friendship. The essayist showed that she had a high ideal, much higher than that of the easy-going soul—be was of the male sex. of course—who, when asked what he would do if he lost a friend, said he should go to the coffee house and find another. One must have friends : "But of all plagues, good Heaven, thy wrath can send, Save, save, oh save me from the candid friend."

Owing to the death of Mr. Warrington Wood it would seem that the promised statue of the Queen, at Warrington, is to remain a promise. This is not as it should be. If thie reason given for the collapse was the illness of the Mayor it would be more intelligible and more satisfactory. Dr. Mackie is not, unhappily, in a condition to consider any- thing in the nature of business; but if he should be restored to health, as it is to be hoped he will, it is not too much to say that he would be the first to repudiate the suggestion that his promise could not be kept because of the death of the sculptor. No doubt he would wish to honour the late Mr. Warrington Wood. but the main object was to nonour Her Majesty and confer a benefit , on the town.

DRIVING A MOTRER INTO HER GRAVE.—Sainuel Hodg• , kinsen, a young man, appeared at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday to answer a charge of threatening to beat and illtreet his father, Frederick Hodgkinson, a baker, who lives in Beamont-strest. The prosecutor said his son did not live with him, but he continually annoyed.him. On the 16th inst., the efetielant went to the house, challenged his father out to fight, and after cursing hint threatened to use violence towards him. The defendant by his conduct was driving his mother into her grave, and that was the reason the prosecutor asked for the protection of the court. The defendant's young sister gave corroborative testimony. The defendant said he had "done nothing to the man." All he wanted was to go into the house seine as his brothers and sisters, but his father denied him. Ceptain Willis said his father had a perfect right to do so if he chose, and he had no right to annoy him. The defendant went to gaol for a fortnight in default of finding sureties for his good behaviour for three months NARROW ESCAPE OF A WESTON POINT GENTLEMAN.— Last • night week Mr. Hugh Wharton, of Weston Point, had a narrow escape from drowning in the c enel at Weston Point. Mr. Wharton, wno is an elderly gentleman of independent means, had been prying a visit to the house of his daughter-in-law, which is situated within his own grounds. The night was very foggy. ared on leaving the house Mr. Wharton had the greatest difficulty in .diseerning any object more than a few yards in front. He apparently lost the path, and instead of turning towards his residence he unwittingly shaped his coerse towards the canal. After walking some yards he stumbled over a low hedge and fell head foremost down toe embankment, rolling upon the canal bank. On rising to his feet, Mr. Wharton, in the darkness, walked into the canal, and was in imminent peril of his life. His cries for help brought some boatmen to the spot, who lost no time in rescuing the unfortunate gentleman. Several persons in the vicinity were also attracted by the cries, and Mr. Wharton was carried hems in a most ex- hausted state. We are glad to say he is now making fav- ourable progress. The painful circumstances attending the death of the lad Twiss, whose dead body was found lyieg close to the outran of the sewer from the chemical works on the Marsh, on Wednesday week, have called attention to the danger caused by the gases arising from the chemical liquid carried down the sewer inte the Mersey. At the inquest on the body of Twiss, held last Friday by the deputy coroner, Mr. W. T. Husband, the jury made a presentment that at the place named there was a dangerous nuisance. This presentment was forwarded by Mr. Husband to the Noxious Vapours In- spector, Dr. Affieck, and the Medical Officer of Health for the district, Dr. Cooper, with the result bleat on Thursday afternoon an inspection was made of the out-fall of the sewer. In addition to the officers named there were present at the inspection, Dr. O'Reeffe, Chairman of the Health Committee, Mr, Husband, Mr. J. 'l'. Allen (clerk to the Local Board), Mr. Dickson (inspec- tor), and Police-sergeant Clarkson. After an inspection had been made it seemed to be the impression of the visitors that the gases emitted were very dangerous, and it is highly probable that steps will be taken to carry the recommenda- tion of the Noxious Vapours Commissioners that something should be done to prevent the percolation of the liquid through the chemical waste into the trough; and also that the trough should be carried further into the river. SHOCKING DISCOVERY IN THE CANAL AT RUNCORN.— Yesterday, at the public-house of Mr. Coward, Jiigh-street, Mr. J. E. Worley, deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Annie Johnson, 28 years of age, who had lived with her mother at Massey-bank, Lymm. During the dense fog on Friday night last, Johnson left home with the intention of going to a faymhouse along the canal bank for some milk. A few minutes afterwards a man went to the house, and asked the mother. a bedridden invalid, for a lamp, because Ire had heard cries of some person in the canal. As John- son did not return, it was concluded that she had lost her way and walked into the canal, but although the water was dragged for several days no body could be found. On Thurs- day afternoons boatman named John Jones, employed by Mr. Joseph Jones, of Ellesmere-street, Runcorn, brought the dead body of a woman to the surface of the canal whilet I "squaring " his boat round opposite the Old Soaperv. The body was nude, with the exceptian of a little linen on the chest, and a portion of a corset, even the boots end stock- ings bad been wrenched off. There were also terrible bruises and coarsen the corpse, and one leg was broken, while the ankle of the left foot was dislocated, and the limb turned completely round. This condition of the body which was described by P.C. 'Boyle was attributed by the brother of the deceased, Richard Johnson, to the canal tugs and fiats, 1 as there was no suspicion of foul play. A juryman ex- pressed surprise that the body should have travelled to i Runcorn, but the Coroner said within his experience bodies i had come from Manchester. An open verdict of "Found dead" was returned,

The deceased lady was the second wife of the late Mr. R. Ockleshaw, who died twelve months ago, leaving behind him the deceased I lady but no issue. Mrs. Ockleshaw was highly re- spected by the inhabitants for her philant4ophy. She was also a good supporter of the excelMnt in- fant school, Peniteth, and by her death the inhabi- tants of Penketh will lose a staunch friend. ,As an indiction of the general esteem in which she was held, the blinds of tenants, and friends are drawn down. DRESCOT RURAL DEANERY.—A meeting of VHS body was held on Monday afternoon, in the Dime- ;San Rooms, Commerce-court, Lord-street, Liverpool. The Rev. Canon Stewart presided over a rather thin meeting. The -other gentlemen present included Canon Penrhyn, the Revs. J. C. Pigot, A. A. Nunn, F. C. Trench, and G. W. Lakeinan ; Drs. Cameron and Fitzpatrick; 'Messrs. 11. Cross, W. Busby, jun., F. C. Eccles, and J. E. Jackson. Dr. Cameron strongly opposed the Church House scheme. It would be enormously expensive, and be like a white elephant to the church, and it would not be suppor- ted by the laity. It looked to him like a gigantic job, with an architect at the bottom of it. .While the clergy in Liverpool were in a state of poverty it would be foolish to spend £200.000 on a gimcrack palace inLondon that would be of no use to any- body. He thought, at all events, that the needs of their clergy should be placed in the forefront. He move-d—‘• That in the opinion Of this meeting, some effort should be made to relieve the necessities of the parochial clergy as a more fitting scheme than the proposed Church House." Dr. Fitzpatrick seconded, stating that Dr. Cameron had expressed what entirely coincided with his views.—The Rev. F. C. Tronch proposed another amendment—" That this conference, while wishing to support the Church House scheme as proposed by those in authority,thinks it is desirable that there should be at the same time a diocesan jubilee memorial for the purpose of augmenting the stipends of the clergy."—This eventually became the substantive motion, and was carried.

January 17, 1887, sherreth,—That your memorialists believe that the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday is, productive of most serious injury to the community. That Lb. prohibition by Parliament of such sale in Scotland, Wales, and the greater part of Ire. land..as well as similar legislation in our principal colonies,. has been attended with most beneficial results. That the canwasses of lonseholders, the declarations of magistrates, and petitions to Parliament from Town Councils, Boards of Guardians, and from millions of the people, show that an immense proportion of the inhabitants of England earnestly desire Sunday closing legislation for their own country. That the working classes, for whose convenience Sunday sale is said to be especially permitted, have, by overwhelm- Mg majorities, expressed themselves in favour of Sunday closing. Your memorialists, therefore earnestly and respect.. fully request your support Of the Bill tor Stopping the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors throughout England daring the .whole of Sunday."
The custom4y votes of thanks concladed the proceed. logs.
RuNCORN RURAL SANILARY AUTHORITY. . .

The usual fortnightly meeting of this body was held in the Board-room at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday after- noon, Lisut.-Colonel Ashton presiding. There were also present the Revs. J. Lockwood and .I. W.. N. Tanner, Messrs. Aaron, Stokes, Brandreth, Mclntyre, W. Whitlow. Campkin, Percival, Lowe, Hewitt, W, H. Llnaker (deputy clerk), and Fartiogton (inspector of nuisances). A ciDIEPLAINT.—The Deputy Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board enclosing copy of a communica- tion received by that Board from certain inhabitants of 'Weston Point with regard to the state of the roads in that locality. The attention of the Authority was also drawn to section 150 of the Public Health Act, 1575, under which an Ui ban Sanitary Authority were empowered to call upon the owners to make up private streets upon which their property abuts, and, on the default of tbe owners, to do the work at their cost. It was open to any Rural Sanitary Authority to apply to tbe Board, under section 276 of the Public Health Act" to declare that section to be in force in any part of their district. At the same time, it was not the Board's practise to issue an order declaring section 150 of the Act to be in force in any part of a rural sanitary dis- trict, except as regarded specified streets, and then only in cases where the streets had been sewered, and except the Rural Sanitary Authority agreed to declare the streets to be highways, under Section 152 of the Act, as soon as they had been put into a proper condition and spoiled to the Board that the latter section might also be put in force with that object, having previously come to a distinct understanding with tbe. highway authorities that they will be willing to take the roads under their charge as soon as the necessary works had been executed. The letter that had been sent to the Local Government Board pointed out the bad condition of certain roads at Weston Point. A meeting of ratepayers had been held, at which it was resolved to ask the Dares- bury Highway Board if they could give any assistance, but they could do nothirguctil the roads were put in repair by the property owners. With one exception, the owners were prepared to do their share of the work.—Mr. Aaron said that the road was in a most disgraceful state.—After a short discussion, it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Mclntyre, that the clerk write to the Daresbury Highway Board, asking would that authority be prepared to take over the roads in question when made good. . _ _

MEDICLL OFFICER'S REPORT.—The Medical Officer (Dr. Adams), in a special report, mentioned the occurrence of a case of diphtheria at Frodsham. He had visited and inspec- ted the premises, and the inspector of nuisances had made an independent examination, and they had failed to detect such sanitary defects as could account for the disease ; it had probably been contracted elsewhere. There was no ex- tension of the disease; the patient was convalescent, and all the usual precauthes to prevent extension were being carefully observed. No other cases of zymotic disease were known by him to eel within the district. Dr. Adams also submitted his quarterly report. Daring the quarter ending December 31, 186, he said, the registrars' returns recorded 133 births and 80 deaths in the four registration sub-districts comprised in the rural sanitary district of the Runcorn Union. IN the births 53 were males and 75 were females, the hirth-rate being 61:3 per 1,000 per quarter (or 264 per 1,000 per annum), compared with 125 births' with a birth-rate of 6.3 per 1,000 per quarter (or 23 2 per 1,000 per annum) in the corresponding quarter of 1885. Of the deaths, 49 were males, and 31 were females, the death-rate being 40 per 1,000 per quarter (or 16-0 per aunum), com- pared with 78 deaths, with a death-rate of 39 per 1,000 per quarter (or 156 per 1,000 per annum) in the corresponding quarter of 1835. Of the deaths 16 occurred in persons under one year of age ; 7 occurred in persons between the ages of 1 and 5 years; 35 in persons between the ages of 5 and 60 years ; and 22 in persons of 60 years of age and up- wards. It would be observed that the death-rate was very satisfactory—t6o per annum. Zymotic diseases caused eight deaths, two being from typhoid fever, one from measles, one from diphtheria one from dysentery, two from diarrhoea, and one from rheumatic fever. This was all the business of interest.

SUNDAY CLOSING MEETING AT WIDNES. On Monday night a public meeting under the auspices of the Central Association for stopping the sale ef Intoxica- ting Liquers on Suuday' was held in the Baths Assembly Room: There was a fair attendance considering the stormy stateof the weather. Captain H Brunner occupied the chair,"and read letters of apology for non-attendance from the Rev. W Bryant, 3 Brock, J.P . B Brown, and T Snape. All the gentlemen expressed sympathy with the object of of the meeting. • At a later period of the evening, a letter was received from the Rev. G Bond, Vicar. of Farnwortb, who said he thoroughly approved of the Sunday Closing Movement, especially in the evening, and only wished that the Sunday closing of all the works in Widnes could also be brought about. In the course of a few remarks the Chairman said in the first instance Mr. 'I. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., had been asked to preside over that gathering, bat he excused himself be- cause he would not be in the country at the time. This question of Sunday Closing was one upon which Mr. Edwards-Moss also said he had net altogether made up his mind, and he wished to give the subject some study be- fore he came to a decision. He (the Chairman) considered the subject of the greatest importance, and in the year of jubilee, upon which we had entered, he did not think that we could raise a better memorial of Her Majesty's reign than by making a strong resolution and keeping that resolu- tion, that in feture we would be a saber people. (Ap- plause.) The Rey. J. Wright Williams, Vicar of Widnes, moved, " That this meeting considers the sale of intoxicating liquors on Lord's Day is unfair, injurious, and ought not to be sanctioned by law." In expressing his full concur- rence with the words of the resolution, the Vicar trusted that in any legislation on the subject, the clubs where at any time a man by some spurious and fictitious pretence could get drink at any time would net be lost sight of (Hear, bear.) Sunday closing should not stop at the pub- lic house. He thought that any secular employment, whether it be at the lame works or the small shops was calculated grievously to affect those engaged in it, and he felt that it would be just as true, although not so keenly true, that all great establishments which made their people work on Sunday were unfair and injurious, and ought not to be sanctioned. (Applauee.) The opponents of Suneay closing had one great cry, "You must not rob the poor man of his beer." (Laughter.) They might rob a man of his comfort, of his virtue, of his wife's love ; rob him of the hearts of his children, and the respect of his fellow men and the respect of his own heart all of which drink did, but fot God's sake they must not rob a poor man of his beer. (Applause.) Mr. James Hargreaves seconded the resolution, and attri- buted much of the Sunday drinking to the manner in which wages were paid. The works of Messrs. Gossage and Messrs. Matthieson had a remarkably sober and steady set of men, whilst in other works there ,was hardly a week but one or two furnaces had to stand. because men were at the police court answering charges of drunkenness. He found that those works that had sober men paid their men's Imes on Friday night, and those that had drunken men invari- ably paid on Saturday. Was this a mere matter of coinci- dence, or was there a cause and effect. A man who got his wages on the Friday night had not time to get drunk, and dare not, because he had to be at his work next morning, and on Saturday his wife would take jolly goad care that he had no money to get drunk with. (Laughter and ap- plause.) At the same time that they all should do their utmost to stein the tide of Jrunkenness, Government ought to restrict the facilities for self-destruction which existed on every hand. (Applause.) The Rev. James Davies, of St. David's Church, Dyer- pool, supported the resolution in place of the Rev. Canon McNeile, who was unable to be present He ieferred to the great prowess made by the temperance movement in re- cent years, and to tbe great benefits that bad resulted from Sunday closing in Scotland, Wales, and a portion of Ire- land. They must not, he said, have men in Parliament who had not yet made up their minds on this question. (Applause.) It was simply a farce te send a man to Par- liament to represent them, and then for that representative to shrug his shoulders and vote as be thought proper. Re- presentatives ought to do as their constituents wished and they might depend upott it that the democracy would find those who would .do as they asked. (Applause.) The tendeocy of the age was to do away, with every institution which could not justify its exis-

tence. He would apply that test to the drink traffic, and especially to the drink traibc on the Lord's day, which had been upon its trial for years. Had the drink traffic in Eng- land justlfied its existence 2 (No.) He was sure the answer " No, no" would come from the rcaffold, the work- house, apd from he depths of poverty and vice. Therefore cut it down, and as it was a creature of the law cut it down by the law. (Applause.) The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. S. Owens moped " That this meeting demands for England the same prohibition of the.traffi a in intoxicating liquors during the whole of Lord's Day as in other parts of the United Kingdom and many of our colonies, and that a petition to Parliament to this effect be adopted and signed by the Chairman." The motion was seconded by the Itt.y. R. Burdon, and carried. Mr. S. B. Stringer moved, and Mr. T. S. Swale seconded, a resolution to the effect that the chairman be requested,to

there was a goodly coMpany of the members of this class on Wednesday evening, in the rooms of the society in Bruns- wick-street. The minister occupied the chair, and the seats reserved for lady members were fully occupied. The un- usual attendance was owing to the presence of the Rev. R. F. Hornabrook, of Halton, who delivered a lecture on "Travels in South Africa." The reverend lecturer gave a brief account of his voyage to the Cape of Good Hope and his journeys in the interior of Ins dark continent. In do- ing so he looked particularly upon the humorous side of all the accidents that befel him and had soon the whole class in a constant ripple of laughter. which was maintained throughont the whole evening. The lecturer gave much good advice to those who intend to become travellers on the sea and to see " Afric's sunny fountains," and forewarned all such that they would meet with difficulties and dangers which they little dreamt of. The gigantic venomous spider " Tarautular," and the wiles of the horsesharper were per- Ocularly dwelt upon as two depredators with which every arrival at the Cape must at last come in centac,„ with and often to their great loss. The lecture concluded with a de- scription of the "accidents of a night," which almost rival the" naixedness " of the two dominoes in the "Comedy of error's." A unanimous vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Hornabrook on the motion of Mr. Bisbrown, seconded by Mr. Dawson. FREE TEA AT ST. LIME'S CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—On Wednesday eve,ning the scholars and a number of poor people from the neighbourhood of Mason, Pennington, and Norton-streets, were treated to a substan- tial tea in Sc. Luke's Chapel. On this occasion none but the most regular and faithful scholars were allowed an abso- lutely free repast, all irregular and truant scholars beine ad- mitted only on payment of a few pence. The tables speedily fined up and 150 lads and lasses with hunger written in their faces threatened the exhaustion of a well-stmed larder. But shops not being far away, a fresh supply was obtained, and when the cloths were removed all wants had been satis- fied. The officers and teachers thankfully acknowledge the kindness of Dr. Robinson, Belvedere; Messrs. J. liandiev,J.P., Garston •, F. Fairhurst, Southport; John Williams, Green. way Meadows ; and Edwin Tockey, Top Locks, Runcorn; by whose generous donations the entire expenses were de- frayed. After tea an interesting entertainment was given by the scholars and teachers, which consisted of competi- tions in singing, recitations, and reading. Mr. J. J. Speak- man presided, and, in his opening addrese, gave some in- teresting reminiscences of the school as he knew it five and twenty years ago. Mr. G. Lacy, Mrs. Hughes, and Miss Heatherington contributed greatly to the interest of the pro- ceedings by their excellent rendering of several soles. Mr. F. Bsci:, in the course of the evening, gave a very stirring and effective speech on " The king's sons" Tee ladies Presiding at the tables were Mrs. Powell, Mrs. II Lacy. Mrs. Hughes, and the Misses Owen. It should be stated that Mr. James Ailzenhead adjudicated in the competitions. Mr. George Lacy accompanied. A very pleasant evening was brought to 3 close by the usual votes of Oa ir ke, which were proposed by Mr. Joseph Slade, and ,O2C01:1 LE`.l he Inn raetor (Rev. J. D. Thomas).

div.head: WESLEYANS AND THE LATE EARL IDDEBLEIGH.
div.p: WESLEYANS AND THE LATE EARL IDDEBLEIGH.

Preaching in St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday morning last, the Rev. W. L. Hunt, of Didsbury College, Manchester, thus referred to the late Earl of Iddes. leigh Whilst we believed, said Mr. Hunt. in guarding the pulpit from any discussion of party politics, we are sure that no shadow of controversy will arise in any mind when we say how sincerely we regret the 9udden removal of the late of Lideslvigh. We do not this morning think of him as the leader of a party, but we remember him as a scholar, a gentleman, and a wise and prudent statesman. The great silent city of thedead is enriched, and the present is impov- erished by his removal from us. We are glad to believe that the Press of this country, both Liberal and Conservative, will willingly bear their tribute to his worth. The tragic circumstances which cluster so closely round his death must affect us all very strongly, and will, I doubt not, enlist the genuine sympathy of the whole nation. We believe him to have been a man of a floe mind, an honest heart, and a clear head, one who loved his God and his fellows, and who served faithfully and well his Queen and country, and one who in the history of the future will be regarded as a great and goad man. ' Whether or no we agree with his politics we must agree that the late earl was one of the most Chris- tian statesmen that ever sat at the Queen's Council or spoke in the English House of .Cominons. We say good-bye to him with sincere regret, and we trust that his spirit may descend upon us. We cannot close the subject without expressing our conviction that the late earl has now entered upon the higher service of the future. Looking at the quiet trisuty of his life, and believing that when a man dies his work is not ended but begun, we exclaim with Mathew Arnold, 0 strong soul, by what shore Tiu lest thou now? . Somewhere surely afar In the sounding labor house vast Of being, is practiced that strength Zealous, beneficlent. firm. Whilst this morning we deeply deplore his loss, we believe that if we take the dust of the present out of our eyes we shall find that his life will prove an inspiration ta .nagy who sorely need it, for God's saints are shining lights, Seen as we go. They are indeed our pillar fires, ' Tnev are that eity'd shining sp'ros We travel to.
