INQUEST AT FRODSHAN.—An inquest was held at the Bear's Paw, Frodsham, on Friday, by Mr. Henry Churton.. coroner for South Cheshire, on the body of Mr. Charles Price, grocer, Frodsham. It appeared from the evidence that the deceased was 49 years of age, and that on the pre- vious forenocn he complained of a severs pain in his side. Shortly afterwards be was found dead on the floor in the closet. The jury, after considering the evidence, returned a verdict of " Died from natural causes; tn wit, syncope."

_ . CEMSHIRE CLERGY AND THE TIFRE QUESTION.—At a recent chapter meeting of the clergy of toe rural deanery of Frodsham, of which the Rev. Canon Greenell, M.A., Rector of Grappenhall, near Warrington, is the rural dean, the fol- lowing resolution, referring to the agitation for the temis- (don of tithes, was passed:—" That the clergy of this rural deanery, in chapter assembled, while sympathizing with the farmers in the present agricultural depression, are of opinion that they would be doing an injustice to their sues- cessors, as well as themselves, if they acceded to any , request for a further reduction of the tithe." ' Tirectr SOCIETY.—A. meeting of the Frodsharn branck of the Religious Tract Society was hell in the Town Hal', Frodsharn, on N'londay, when the Vicar, the Rev. H. B. Biogg, MA., took the chair. In the absence of the secre- tary (Mr. Samuel Ormerod), extracts from the minute book were read, which showed that the branch society was pro- gres4ng very favourably. The total amount of subscrin- ttons, etc., received during the past twelve months was £l9 ts 10.1. The Bev. Charles Suteff ~, vicar of Holy Trinity, Stalybridge, and Mr. Richard Butcher, of Bury, one of the aesociation secretaries of the society, attended al a deputa- tion, and delivered interesting addres:es descriptive of the work carried OD by the society in Japan, India, and China, as well as in this country. Votes of tharks at the close were accorded to the deputation and the chairman, and the meet- ing terminated. Partoenrat COMMITTEES.—At Si meeting of the Froi- sham and 'irodsham Lordship Parochial Committee, held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Friday, Mr. Alfred Thomas in the chair, the question of seeding a deputation to Lon- don to interview the Lordl Government Board in the matter of the,Frodsham Water Scheme was reconsidered on the re- commendation of the Central Authority, and after some discussion the clerk was directed to write to the Local Gov- ernment Board and state that as a tvater supply for Frod- sham id greatly needed, they would be glad to hear what their lor isbips would now recommend to be done. An ac- count was produced from Messrs. FItAtritLENT ENLISTMENT.—Denis McNamara, charged with having fraudulently enlisted in the Liverpool Regi- ment. was sent to prison for seven days, it having been proved that he was a first-class Army Iteserve man, and had served six years with the Gordon Highlanders. DRCNIEENNESS.—dw.rd Crosby, for being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road on the Bth just, and for sinii- la-ly misconducting himself in Buttermarket-street on Sat- nrday night, was tined 15s and costs, or in default of pay- ment three weeks' imprisonment with hard labour.—Thomas Miskell and Dominick Knockton were each fined 5s and costs for drunkenness. IN SEARCH OF THE SHIP CANAL. —Thomas Bap, lag from Salford, was brought up as a person of unsound mind, be having been found wandering in Liverpool-road on Saturday at noon. When accosted by a policeman, who had noticed that he wore clothing belonging to the Salford Union, he said that be had come to Warrington because he had heard they were going to make a ship canal there. He was remanded in older that a reply to a communication sent to Salford Union might be received. He was afterwards taken back to Salford. BEGGING. Browne, who pros cuted, said the defendant was a tenant of Mr. John Platt, who owned a number of houses about Lythgoe's-lane, and had a great deal of trouole with his tenants; and that case had been brought as a warning to others, that they could not go away in the night time, tak- ing their goods wiiile they were owing rent. Last Monday the complainant put the bailiffs In possession, but by some means they wets tot outside. On the evening of the tot- 'wing day it was found that the goods had been removed. —The defendant said he had not been in constant work.— The complainant said he believed the bailiffs had been promised that a sovereign would be paid, and they were ' treated to some beer.—An order Was made for the payment of £2, at the rate of 5s per week.

RECKLESS DRIVING (;;--A TRACTION Exame.—John Hat- chinson was summoned for driving a locomotive on the highway at Lymm, at a greater speed than four miles an hour.—Mr. Jenkios (Warrington) appeared for the defence. A sergeant of tte Lymm police said that the traction engine was being driven by de endant at a speed of eight miles an hour. The engine travelled over a mile and a quarter in ten minutes. Bills of fire were flying out of the funnel ; witness never saw an engine driven so recklessly before. Defendant, and two others who were with him, were run- ning to keep up with the engine.-1 witness named O'Neil, a labourer, said that as he was driving on the road in ques- tion theengine overtook him; the men were running at the side.—Mr. Jenkins pleaded guilty on 13-quelf of his client, who was fined 203 and costs, all, £2 13s 6. bright children. He pointed out that this increased fee would at present only mean about £2O to the Board, and he asked was it worth while to upset these arrangements, which had worked so extremely well, for the sake of that miserable sum. This proposition that fees should be higher in the Board schools than in the Denominational schools would be unfair to The former. He thought it highly un- desirable that any element of discord should be thrown in- to the working of the Board. (Hear, hear.) They had got on for many years extremely amicably. It had been recog- nised by the Denominationalists that the School Board had carried out its policy with the utmost consideration for them, and with the utmost fairness, and they who bad identified themselves more with the School Board expected they would he treated with the same fair- ness and consideration. He implored them with all the earnestness he could not to do anything he could not to do anything which would upset the extremely harmonious work of the past. • The very best Government Inspector they ever had, Mr. Scott Coward, bad put it on record that the School Board of Widnes had set an example of energy and efficiency, coupled with economy which other school boards in the districts would do well to imitate. There were no better schools in the kine,dom, and he should be extremely sorry if there was anything done to diminish their efficiency. As he believed this motion calculated to do so be should vote against it. Mr. Davies protested against any obstacle being placed in the way of the education of the children. Mr. liaison stated the poor children left school before they reached the seventh standard, and argued that they educated in that standard children whose parents could pay for their attendance at a grammar school or some of the , higher schools. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Wareing declared that after weighing the atgaments ' pro and con he should vote against the motion. He could conceive that the increase in the scale of fees would have no other result than to drive children out of the echool, and thus reduce its efficiency. The only forecast he could givA . was that the children would desert the Boaid Schools and go into the Denominational Schools. Dean Finegan asked how many children in the advanced standards were unable to pay for themselves. (Hear, bear.) If this queetion were anawered as it could be answered, they would find that there was no fey. Mr. Timmis hid , no right to assume that they were introducing an element of discord into this Board—(hear, hear)—and lie rezretted that a chairman,whose words were so much re.pacted bynone more than himself, should have thooLttht fit to mike such an , assertion. Mr. Timmis said their province was to deal with the education, but 39 to rates they had nothm.e to do with them. Ile asked Mr. Timmis why he did not say so in his address to the ratepayers. The Chairman said his statement was that education was the Board's first consideration ; the rates the second. Dean Finegan said that was substantially the some. If they would take a walk along the lanes they would see shining clearly, after all the snow and smoke, the words " efficiency and economy" in the remnants of the addresses on the walls. (Laughter.) But the first effort the com- mittee had made on the side of economy was met by an im- putation of motives to which he ohpcted. The Chairman admitted that his remarks were out of order, but he thought they would not object to what he had to say, and lie was obliged to them for listening to them. The motion was carried by seven votes to four. The gentlemen for were—Rond, Finegan, Heyes, Clarke, "[rai- son, Bradshaw, O'KeeHe ; against, the Chairman, Deacon, Wareing. and Davies. TEACHERS' EARNINGS REDUCED.—HOPELESS OPPOSITION.

The School Management Committee also recommended the displacemeat of the present scale of salaries by one which was given at length in the agenda. The only altera- tion, however, was made in the system of bonuses. As there were many matters of detail the Chairman sue- gested that it would be well for the Board to resolve itself into committee so that they could be disceseed with greater freedom, and therefore better understood. Some discussion took place upon this suggestion, to which Dean Finegan ob- jected. At the instance of the Chairman, however, Dean Finegan made some general observations why there should be an alteration in the system in fcrce. Under the old scheme, he said, the Beard paid head teachers a bonus of 2e per cent. on their salaries on results of 80 per cent. A master or mistress, however, would not remain two years in the Board's service if only 80 per cent, were passed, and the committee considered it absurd to give a prize for what they would dismiss a teacher for only attainine. Ninety per cent, was now as easy to attain as 80 per cent. was when the system W9B established with regard is class Eubjects such as sewing, which the teachers were bound to teach, the committee saw no reason to give a bonus. The payment for spec;fic subjects the committee did not propose to change because they were extra, and to encourage the masters and mistresses to teach them, they allowed a bonus of 23 per cent. on'the grant. The Rev. G. Bond expressed himself in favour of the re- duction. The Chairman said the general operations of the proposal was to make certein deductions from the total earnings of the teachers. From the inquiries be had made he did not think the head teachers were r vernal', and be knew that denominational teachers were mid quite as much, and some got more, and they were not more efficient. Dean Finegan said it was easy to make an ex-parte etate- ment. In many instances the salaries paid in Board Schools. were twice as much as those paid in denominational schools, and he could support his assertions by strong evi- dence. The Chairmen was mentioning cases at Woolton and Carlton, when • Dean Finegan exclaimed: Garston and. Wool ton ! Where they don't know what to do with their money? The Chairman: They always dun ma for a subscription, nevertheless. , Dean Finegan said in the Widnes Board Schools they had one master receiving about £240 and another 11220. Mr. Deacon characterised the new scheme as the old one with a bit snipped out here and a bit snipped out there, and pointed out that the old scheme had only been adopted two , years on the suggestion of the School Management Commit- I tee, which at that time had Dean Finegan and Mr. Irnison for members. He had beard no valid reason for a change from Dean Finegan. He would accept that gentleman's statement that 90 per cent was as easy to attain as 80 was formerly, but no equivalent was given in the new scheme pay ter 90 per cent what was paid for 80, and make a higher standard of 95 per cent. Drawing, he believed, was now made a class subject, and in consequence it was now pro- posed to deduct the 25 per cent of that grant formerly paid to the reacbers from the teachers eatery. That was a clear reduction of salary, arid they had no reasons given them to warrant the alteration. Dean Finegan said it was quite as easy to get an excel- lent report now as it was to get a good report when the old system was established, and for that reason the Committee proposed to give 5 per cent for excellent, and to give no bonus for good, because they expected good. In the senior and junior schools the Beard gave a bonus of 5 per cent. if 90 per cent passed, and if only 80 per cent passed, a bonus of 24- per cent. The Committee proposed that if 95 per cent. passed to give a bonus of 3 per cent on the amount of the year's salary. Then they discontinued the bonuses for clan I subj-cts because the teachers were already paid for teaching those subjects in which he was compelled ts give instruction. In specihc suljects a bonus of 25 per cent, of the grant was paid, and the Committee left that alone, because it was something out of the ordinary course, of education, and , something they wished to encourage. The instruction of pupil teachers was in an unsatisfactory state, and that was left over for consideration until after the examination in April. Mr. Deacon remarked that he could not take any great credit for the old scheme. Father Clarke and he were as- sociated on the Committee, and he was quite willing to share any praise or blame with him. He added that the effect of this new scheme would he a reduction of salaries, and he could not vote in favour of it. Father Clarke objected in tote to bonuses. He attributed a great deal of the overpressure of which they had heard lead complaints to this system of bonuses. With regard to salaries, he thought the teachers were very well paid, and quite as well as any teaching staff in England. The aver- age salaries for head teachers in denominational schools throughout the country were between £l4O and £l5O, and he thought the School Management Committee was dealing very leniently with the teachers. The salaries had hitherto been too high, and he should vote on that issue. The Rev. G. Bond agreed with the committee's recom- mendations, as did Mr. Imison.

The Chairman said Father Clarke had put the matter very succinctly, that he considered the salaries were too high. He had another clear idea, that they were not too high, and he objected to their being lowered. Dean Finegan had cer- tainly given a good reason for having an alteration made in the limit of 80 per cent., but he asked the Board to consider the general question—Was it worth while to upset the ex- cellent teachers they had got after they had got such admirable results by asking them to tike lower salaries? . _

If his calculation Was right the reduction would amount to £lO4 3s 4d, and concern 14 head teachers. Last year the Sicam's Cross head teachers, Mr. Showan's department, earned .21s 2d per head, the Warrington-road head master 20e 3d, and at West Bank Mr. &toddy, highest of all, with 21s sd. At Simm's Cross there were three excellents, two good; at Warrington-road, one excellent, two good, one fair; and at West Bank, three excellent and two good. These were most exceptional returns. By diminishing the salaries of the teachers they would probably diminish their zeal and decrease their grant from the Government, and conse- quently the ratepayers would really pay more. Mr. Davies said the reward the teachers were to rec.live

for their most successful -ia-bo-u;s Wa's—t-crise. a- reduction of salaries, and he thought it was ungenerous and unwise, be- cause they would only discourage the teachers, and they should not have such good results. Tlqa tendency of the resolution proposed was to lower the Board Schools to the level of the voluntary schools. (Cries of "I object" from Dean Finegan and Father Clarke,) He did not wish to impute motives. Dean Finegan asked that that expression should be with- drawn, and at the request of the Chairman Mr. Davies withdrew ths objectionable expression. Mr. Reyes objected to bonuses altogether as he con- sidered they were bad in principle. De4lll Finegan protested against being singled out as doing all this. He was simply the mouthpiece of the com- mittee. They heard about schools self-supporting, and in the nnat breath :the ratepayers were to be asked to pay £13,800 for education. What became of self-suoporting schools uncaer such circumstances. As ratepayers they had a right to protest, and as a ratepayer he did protest. The Chairman moved an amendment that for" excellent" in the infants' school a bonus of 10 per cent be paid instead of 5 proposed.
Mr. Deacon seconded, Me. Am en (-talent was lnst by 7 vat..s to 4.

The original propoiition was thee put and carried, the voting again being seven to four. Those far were—Dean Finegan. Father Clarke, Rev. Cf. Bond. Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Reyes, Bradshaw, and Imison ; against, the Chairman, MeeBTS. Davies, D ' eacon and Wareint, THE FREE DINNERS.

The School Management Committee—had—received a letter from Mr. S. B. Stringer asking for the free 084 of a room at the schools in which to supply free dinners to needy child- ren, and the following, reply had been sent :—"That the committee, by the rules of the Board. are excluded from let- ting any rooms in any of the schools otherwise than by the scale of bite laid down for their guidance. The Chairman submitted a letter from Mr. Stringer, who pointed out that the free-dinner movement was entirely un- sectarian, and be hoped the Board would grant him tbi small favour of a room at Warringtondroad School. After some discussion, the Chairman gave notice that at the next meeting he would move a resolution giving discre- tionary power to let the rooms free for unsectarian pur- poses. .

matched their opponents. The northerners evidently had a liking for an open game, and the ball was kept on the move, and this was no doubt good tactibs on their part, for Warrington generally had a decided advantage in the scrimmages. Amongst the cup-holders Barnes was again the hero of the occasion. owing to his dodgy runs and cleverly dropped goal. Fair Turner was also to the fore and made more than one of his all but irresistible rushee. Among the forwards Povey also came in for a good deal of deserved commendation, as did Rigby, while Davies and Ashton were well to the fore. Jolley played a particularly determined game, and Massey on the other wing was dash- ing as anal. Appleton continues to win favour as full back, and on Saturday he did nothing ty impair his rema- tation. Of the visiting team, Little, Alexander. Leak-c, Harley, Woodburn, and Walton may be specially men- tioned.

Turner Hayes, Davies, Littlewood, Potter, Rigby, Dillon, and Ashton. Bar- row: Full back, Woodburn ; three-quarter backs, Forshaw. Harley (captain). Gregory; half backs. Walton and Rolab ; forwards, Little. Myeracougb. Alexander, McVeigh, Holt, Baines, Leake, Ferguson, and Rogerson. ASSOCIATION RULES.

LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT V. CRESIIIRE.—Teams repre- sewing the Che:hire and Liverpool and District Football Associations met at Crewe on Saturday afternoon, and a capital game resulted in a victory for Liverpool by two goals to one. The goalkeeper for the winner was T. Cham- pion, of the Earlestown Club, who displaved considerable ability, and W. Allison, of the Earlestown Club, played ex- ceedingly well on the left wing. 'The remainder of the team was selected from the Everton and Bootle Clubs. WIGAN AN DISTRICT FOOTBALL ASSOCIATION.—A meet- ing of the Wigan and District Football Association was bald at Wigan on Friday evening, when a protest arising out of the Hindley v. Golborne cup tie was received, but its con- sideration was left over to a future meeting. The draw for the semi-final ties of the cup competition afterwards took place with the foilewing result :—Hindley or Goltorno v. Earlestown ; Haydock v. Westhoughton Reserve. The matches have to be played on neutral grounds on or before February 12th.
NOTES BY THE WAY.

About the smartest piece of play was the goal dropped by Barnes from a piss by the foot from Massey, the little centre popping it over the bar in the twinkling of an eye. Speakman's form daring the past two or three matches has wonderfully improved, his pecaliar style ef passing being exceedingly embarrassing to his opponents, bat not 80 to Jolley, who takes them splendidly, and is rapidly gainin,, for himself the name of one of the best wing three•quarters In the west of the shire.

_ We bear that the committee of the Warrington Football Club have nominated Memsrs.•Fair, Turner, Barnes, and Gilbert for the county match against Durham, at Liverpool, on Saturday next. Let ms hope that the County Committee will give one or more ef the trio a trial, an all are well wortb it.

At the half-yearly audit of the accounts of the Warring- ton Football Club, it was found that the club are in a very flourishing condition, having considerably over £lOO to the good. This sneaks very well for the manner in which the secretary, treasurer, and the gentlemen on the committee carry out their work, and the way in which the game is patronised in Warrington. . . _
4 Warrington journey to Mosslev to-day, and if the team turns up to expectation they will give a good account of themselves.

Warrington added another laurel to their already pretty full chaplet by their defeat of Barrow on Saturday. The match was a very good one from a spectator's point of view, there being a goodly number of lively incidents which bad the effect of keeping up the excitement. This was not a little due to the plucky manner in which the Barrovians fought against adversity. They seemed as though they entirely refused to recognise defeat, and although long be- fore the finish it appeared to most people to be a hopeless battle they struggled on to the very end with undiminished determination. In the case of this match, it can be said without hesitation 'that the better team won, for nothing could be plainer than that the visitors were just a little too light for the task they had undertaken. Among the ties for the first round of the West Lanca- shire Junior Cap that have been played off are the follow- ing :—Lymm beat Warrington St. Paul's by twelve points to four ; Pemberton, one goal. six tries, and eight minors to Lowe House nothing; Elgr3bill beat Waterloo St. John's by one goal, two tries, and tire minors to none. In Association circles, the great tie between Preston North End v. Renton, which has been several times postponed, came on for decision on Saturday, the place ef contest being the Renton ground* On arrival at the park the ground was found to be frozm as hard as iron, and, after careful inspec- tion, Mr. Betts ruled that it was totally unfit for a Cap tie, and it was agreed to play a friendly match only. Amid cries of " Play the tie," and threatening remarks, the ball was started by Thompson and soon rushed through by Renton. "Off side" was, however, claimed, and the goal was dis- allowed. The crowd now rushed in by the hundred, and after a vain attempt to clear the field, it was resolved to go on with the Cup tie, under a protest. Final result: North End, 3 goals; Renton. 3 goals.

div.head: P.RBSCOT LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: P.RBSCOT LOCAL BOARD.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians wee held on 'Thursday in the Boardroom of Whiston Workhouse, Mr. John Lowe pvesided, and there were also present—MetaSte. G B Johnson, J Barchall, W Middlehurst. E Syder, J Ellison, J Whalley, W Tyrer, J M Wareing, ar Leatherbarrow,J /tensor', J Fisher, W G Ashton, J Jackson, J Buckley, P Middlehurst, H flulmeeT Eatock, C W Wool, Thomas Chambers. T Beall, W B Longton, and S H Hart- ley (clerk). HOIME STATISTICS.—The Workhouse Master (Mr. Hale) reported that there were 524 inmates this week, against 523 last week, and 458 in the corresponding period of last year. Vagrants relieved 30, corresponding period last ye tr 36. REGISTRATION Fgars.—A communication was read from the Local Government Board stating that they bad paid to Mr. C. C. White, the treasurer of the Union, the sum of £3l 10e, the amount repayable from the grant made by Parliament in respect of fees paid to the registrar of births and deaths for the period ending 29th September, 18S6. APPLICATION FOR INCREASED SALARY.—Miss Ada Bar- ton, organist at the Workhouse chapel, applied for an in- crease of salary. She stated that she was approaching the completion of her third year of such office, and explained that she had to attend 168 Protestant services, 106 Catholic services, 52 Protestant practices, and 52 Catholic practices— an average of 378 yearly. The matter was referred to the Finance Committee.—The Clerk stated that the 'Local Government Board had intimated that it was not competent for the Guardians to subscribe £33 to the Liverpool society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. He (the Clerk) had sent the communication to the secretary of the society. and they hoped to prevail upon the Local Government , Board to grant it, believing they could if they would do so. • THE WATER SUPPLY TO THE WORKHOUSE. . The Clerk read a communication from Mr. J. J. Brown, ' of Prescot, stating that the Liverpool, London, and Globe , Insurance Company held the Guardians covered to the ex- • tent of £27,350 !n respect of the Workhouse buildings, &c, and that a new policy was to be prepared and forwarded as . soon as possible.—Rev. Thomas Chambers (Haiewood) who had given notice of his intention to move "That steps be . taken for immediately providing an adequate supply of water to the Workhouse to be available in the event of fire." said he thought it a happy coincidence that this motion was down for a dav on which the clerk had read such a commu- nication from the Insurance Company. At a meeting held a short time 54ors, when it was arranged to insure the now I buildings, Mr. Wareing said—" The lives of the inmates were more Yalnable than the buildings. It was a curious state of things to increase the insurance policy and yet take no 'measures to protect the inmates." To thosieremarks the clerk then replied that "they could not get the Guardians to obtain a sufficient supply of water, but if a fire should arise and he (the clerk) had not attended to the proper insur- ance of the building, and if he had not kept the policies apace with the extension of the buildings he would have baen to blame."—Mr. Chambers s iid he fancied he could see upon the surface of those rematks a complaint against the Guardians, and jus,ly so. He also detected an under- tone of reproach upon the Guardians and justly so. He wanted the Guardians that day to i:eltnit a principle, and that was that while they had gone to the expense of in- creasing the policies upon their new buildings they were justified in protecting the lives of the inmates of that work- house in case of fir& Unhappilly, fires at workhouses were not uncommon things. He believed that since the remarks he had quoted were made there had been fires at two work- houses in the kingdom; and he thought there were those present whose memories would carry them back 22 years or more to the great fire which occurred at Brownlow-hill Workhouse. At that time, notwithstanding all their ad- mirable appliances, some 20 or 30 lives were lost. The ar- rangements were admirable, but there was a hitch in the water supply at the time it was required. He mentioned that to show that fires at workhouses were by no means lICICOMMEM, and when they occurred the consequences were generally dreadful. Why might not a fire occur at the Prescot Union Workhouse? Because they had been spared for so many years from the calamity of a: dis- astrous fire were they to expect immunity for years to come? The probability was that having been spared so long a calamity might be nearer than they anticipated. He there- fore asked the Guardians in pursuance of his notice to do away with the complaint, and remove the reproach which had attached to them fer ten or twelve years. Hiving gone to £4OO or £5OO expense in providing fire appliances, were they to be without water? As practical men he asked them not to dismies the subject as they bad done before, but as men of business he asked them to do their duty, and as Christian men protect the lives of those poor bedridden creatures, and prevent the sacrifice there would undoubtedly be in the event of a fire. He would propose that a commit- tee of the whole Board be formed to consider the matter.— Mr. Wareing, who seconded the motion, said it Seemed to him that if they neglected to provide a proper water supply they would be guilty of a grave and serious crime, and if they were not arraigned—as they might deservedly expect to be —at any rate they would be ex ,crated throughout the length and breadth of the land.—The motion was carried unanimously, and it was decided to hold a private meeting prior to next Board day.

DREADFUL CATASTROPHE IN LONDON. PANIC AT A JEWISH CLUB. SEVENTEEN PERSONS KILLED. . _ _ _

Late on Tuesday night an appalling catastrophe happened at the room of a Jewish dramatic club, 3, Prince's-street, Spitalfields, London, resulting in the loss of seventeen lives. The club is a favourite place of amusement among the Jews of the locality, entertainments being given there almo6t nightly, and on Tuesday night there was a benefit. It is situated in one of the quietest parts of the locality; and has almost the appearance of a private house, being solely for dramatic purposes. The owner is Mr. Smith, a butcher, of Dorset-street, Spitalfields, who has recently laid out £3,000 on decorations and repairs. Various rumours have been circulated respecting the origin of the panic, but it has been clearly shown to have been caused by a man and woman quarrelling outside the building. The wo- man screamed, and someone outside raised the cry of "Fire !" Almost instantaneously the entire audience, numbering some 500, mostly Jews, rushed to the entrance, and in an incredibly short time twelve women, three boys, a girl, and a man were crushed to death. A.policeman, attracted by the noise, summoned assistance, but the chief service that cculd be rendered was to extricate seven per- sons more or less injured. These were conveyed to the London Hospital, but their injuries were not, of so serious a nature as to prevent their being taken to their homes after medical assistance had been rendered.
The scene inside the hall is described as of the most distressing character..

The people were possessed by the mad, unreason- ing instinct of self-preservation, and nothing could restrain them. Men fought with women, women with men, and both sexes with each other to get near the coveted doors leading into the lobby, whence exit was clear to the passage leading to the street. But those doorways, which led in truth to a veritable death-trap, were already hopelessly blocked with fighting and struggling and bleeding men and women, although not a couple of minutes had elapsed since the first alarm. Probably, had the struggle been confined to the doorways leading from the hall itself, calm would have been restored with no more serious results than broken limbs and other serious injuries to person; but someone connected with the management of the hall or with the actors apparently thought that darkness would conclu- sively prove to the maddened audience that there was really no fire, and be therefore turned off the gas at the meter behind the stage. Unhappily, the struggling wretches in the area below were not in a frame of mind to draw logical conclusions, and the darkness served only to add to their terrors. The struggles at the inside doorways, however, les- sened somewhat in violence, for the block seemed to have been removed, and the terrified people were making their way towards thb outside passage; but the crush was fearful, and the cursing and yelling horrible to hear. The women and children suffered terribly, for with very few exceptions their male protectors, if they had any, had left them to shitt for/themselves.

NV Rhin five minutes of the first rush a score of bodies were piled against the partition, and unfor- tunately acted as a barrier to the pressure of the surging torrent behind. It is beyond doubt that the dead would have been numbered by scores had it not been for the presence of mind of the consta- ble on the Prince's-street beat, who, on receiving information of-what was going on inside the club- house, Rounded an alarm, sent off to the nearest police station for assistance, and with one or two volunteers entered the passage leading to the lobby and hall. He quickly took in the situation, and finding it impossible to rescue either the 'dead or the living until the partition had been cleared, he proceeded to demolish it as best he could with his baton. Whilst so engaged, with the willing assist- ance of some of the neighbours, Inspector O'Connor and Inspector :Babington, with a number of men from Leman-street and Commercial-road 'Stations, came upon the scene, and in a few minutes the obstruction was removed, and the frightful scene within revealed' At least 50 men and women lay in heaps on the floor, and many bodies fell into the outer room as soon as the pressure of the Partition had been removed. The people in the ball and on the staircase were still struggling wildly, many of the men with clothing torn from their, backs, and the women bonnetless, bleeding, and dishevelled. The first thing done was to drive back these people until the bodies could be removed, and the police had little difficulty in, enforcing their com- mands, for their presence acted like magic ii*estor- ing confidence, and many of the poor creatures on the floor had, merely fainted or had fallen from exhaustion. Some, however, were -seriously injured, and several gasped wad expired as they were in turn lifted from the heap. When this necessary work had been completed, it was found that there were seventeen corpses, and these were taken into an adjoining room, thezemainder of the audience,.l to the number of about-three hundred, meanwhile 1 leaving the building some shamefacedly, others— and these not a few—still screaming or weeping I hysterically, men and women alike. The dead and injured having been handed over to the care of the numerous doctors who had arrived in response to police summonses, the inspectors proceeded to ex- amine the building. They soon discovered that the gas had, as already stated, been turned off at the stage meter, but it should have been mentioned be- fore that the gas in the lobby was supplied through a separate meter, and the ghastly struggles there took place in full light. The hall itself presented an extraordinary spectacle. Chairs and seats were overturned, many: broken, and allseattered about in fantastic confusion. The floor was strewn with hats, wearing apparel, and certain strange objects which at first greatly puzzled the police, but which it was soon ascertained were wigs, worn, according to the the custom of their country, by Polish Jewesses. Passing down the hall the explorers were suddenly startled by a feeble wail; and investigation resulted in the discovery of a baby. The poor little thing had evidently fallen froth its mother's ariasin the rush and panic, and had rolled under one of the seats, thus saving itself from being tramped to death. 'There it had remained screaming until com- pletely exhausted, and when picked up, could give vent only to the feeblest moans. Kiridly arms were stretched out for the little stranger, and restoratives were administered with immediate benefit, for the infant' smiled feebly upon its tearful nurses, and lisped "Mamma," 'Mamma." Its mother 'was found amongst the.disfigured corpses in the adjoin- ing room. By this time news of the disaster had spread throughout the district, and Prince's-street soon became crowded with weeping and wailing then and women. Those who had lost friends and relatives were surrounded by sympathising but voluble and excited co-religionists, and for half an hour or more the whole street was in an Uproar, but the crowds gradually dispersed, and by one o'clock' the police were left in peaceful possession of the place.

The dead have been laid out in the reading-room of the club, a room cnly about 15 feet by 10 feet. The body of one man betrs not the slightest sign of injury, and it has been ascertained that he died of sheer exhaustion and excitement, brought about by his efforts to rescue those in danger of being trampled to death.

It appears that there was a very large attendance of members of the club, which is used by the Ger- man and Russian Jews in the vicinity, as a benefit performance had been organised by a dramatic society connected with the club in aid of a sick member. The audience numbered from four to live hundred persons, a very large proportion of them being women, while there were many men there with their wives and the whole of their family, Nearly all those present were of the lowest class of Jews—workers in the slopmaking establishments, boot trade, and other industries in which cheap labour is employed. An inspection of the entrance to the hall shows that no precaution has been omitted to avoid a catastrophe such as that which has unfortunately happened. The passage from the ball to the street entrance is nearly ten feet wide where the melee Ncurred. A little nearer the street, which is 'Atached by two pairs of doors, opening either outwards .or in- wards, is a wooden partition containing a couple of swing doors, but these likewise open either way, and are therefore no impediment. The disaster would seem to be attributable, not so much to inadequate means of exit, supposing both doors to have been open, as to the collision of two streams of excited people at a right angle, where the hall and gallery passages meet. The fact of the staircase being also at an angle to the entrance hall tended likewise to aggravate the crush. Of the seventeen persons killed, only one, an aged He- brew, was a man, the remainder being women and children.

• WIDFFS SCHOOL BOARD-
IMPORTANT MEETING.-A REACTIONARY POLICY.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday after- noon at the Offices, Victoria-road ; Mr. T. S. Timmis, J.P., presided, and there were present the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, the Revs, G. Bond, and J. Clarke; 3lessrs. Bradshaw, H. W. Deacon, J. B. Imison, F. Reyes, J. W. Wareing, R. H. Davies, Dr. O'Keeffe, and G. H. Danby.(clerk.),_

div.head: WELCOME TO MR. DAVIES.
div.p: WELCOME TO MR. DAVIES.

The Chairman thought be might say as the mouthpiece of the Board that It was with great pleasure they.saw Mr. Davies again in his place, and expressed the hope that his tour had re•estsblished his health. (Hear, hear.) DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

This committee reported that during December there were 78 applications for the payment of school fees, which were recommended to be paid in 66 cases. There were 284 cases before the committee for contravention of the Education Act. and 53 persons were prosecuted and cmvicted by the magistrates. .

div.head: CHANGE IN THE STARK
div.p: CHANGE IN THE STARK

The School Management Committee accepted the resigna- tion of Mr. E. Robinson, assistant mister, Simms Cross School, and appointed Mr. C. IL Rands in his place, at a ealary of £7O per annum. INCREASED SCHOOL FEES.—A REACTIONARY

div.head: POLICY.
div.p: POLICY.

The School Management Committee recommended that subject to the consent of the Education Department the following scale of fees be charged in the various Board Schools: Infants, 21 per week; standards I and 11, 31 per week; standards 111 and IV, 41 per week; standards V and VI, 61 per week; and for advanced classes, 91 per week. In reply to the Chairman, the Clerk said the present scale of fees was—lnfant schools, 21; junior classes, 311 senior boys and girls, 41; advanced classes, 6d per week. Dean Finegan moved the adoption of the recommendation, and stated that when the existing scale was framed the Board had no advanced classes in the sense that they had advanced classes now. At that time they had scarcely a fourth standard. Within the last few years the Depart- ment had seen well to recommend seven standards. The committee practically left the fees the same up to the sixth standard'; but above that standard they proposed to charge 91 each scholar, with the consent of the Department. The advanced class was one that required a great deal of atten- tion, and one in which the education was of a very high order. He held that the increase would not affect the poor people, as the Board had machinery in force for paying their fees. Whether they were in the first or seventh Stan- dard would make no difference. _ _

Rev. G. Bond said many people objected to educating other peonle's children up to so high a standard, but if they were the people who received the benefit ought to pay a con- siderable amount themselves.

Mr. Deacon, dealing with Dean Finegan's a:gument with regard to poor people, pointed out that the Guardians paid fees on a scale. There was a considerable body of people who could just manage to pay the fees, and whose cases were just beyond the limit fixed by the Guardians, and these persons would be affected by this rise in the scale of fees. Ile could not discover the "very high education" between the 6th and 7th standards that the people mentioned by Mr. Bond appeared to perceive. The Board had always acted with great fairness to the voluntary schools in the matter of school fees. If the Board charged 93 in ;heir ad- vanced classes and the voluntary schools charged 6d, the children would naturally go to the voluntary schools. Another objection he had was one that was felt very severely on the District Education Committee, of which he wee chairman. That committee found that as children were forced into school at an earlier age, and attended school more regularly than they used to do, they got into the higher standards more readily, and there was consequently a larger proportion of children in the higher standards than there was some years ago, and the difficulty of keeping them at school had increased, and if a still higher fee was charged the difficulty would be much greater. They would have a larger number of children about the streets than they had now. He did not think any obstacle should be placed in tho way of these children attending school regularly,and he th refore objected to the raising of the fees. The Chairman did not consider the arguments advanced by Dean Finegan a sufficient reason for raising the fees. He agreed with every word Mr. Deacon had said as to not patting difficulties in the way of educating children. The object of the Board was to educate the poor children of the district' the question of rates was another matter alto- tether. Their business was to educate the children effi- ciently, and as economically as possible with that efficiency. He objected to this increase of fees because they would press hard on the parents of children who were in the ad- vanced classes, and because he believed it to be to the in- terest of the Board, as educators, to get these children in- to those classes. (Rear, hear.) He had a great objection against children leaving school too early, and he should like to ote the lines drawn a great deal harder if it were not for making the demand too bard on the parents. Children left school sadly too soon, and if they handicapped them still further the children would have no inducements to re- main in the higher classes. It was a loss to them as a com- munity, and a loss to us as a nation, to let children go away imperfectly educated. We suffered daily in competition ; with foreigners because they were better educated and bet- ter trained, and he thought it would be a great mistake to put any further impediment in the way of the education of

„ , In the morning Mr. Mackennal took as his text I. Corinthians,. c. 4, part of 4th verse, "He that judgetli me is the Lord.” Dealing with the futility of Inman judgment of Christian work he said that the man who succeeds was almost certain to- be thought worthy of success. If a man only made money he was certain not only of the reputation of a rich, but he was almost certain to have also the reputation of being a wise and a strong man, and perhaps a good man. Yet they all knew that max- im, money even in the commercial world was no test of wisdom. There were very. many things to be taken into consideration—luck, mischances that could not have been avoided, the character of some person in Whom trust had been reposed, the failure or continuance of health—all these things would come in and ought to qualify their estimate even of the wordly 'wisdom of the man who.sBucceeds or falls. What a satire sometimes was the judgment of the world on Church success and individual suc- cess. Sometimes a man received public honour, and men were ready to join in admiration of his good- ness, his excellence, his Christian virtue and devout- ness, while all the time the man knew, that in the days gone by he was better—better in those days when some regarded him with suspicion and many blamed him, and there 'were few who could recog- nise that in the unnoticed and arduous course he was pursuing there was an honest heart and stead- fast purpose and an obedient soul. in the evening the preacher, the Rev. A. Mearns, did net preach from a text, but gave an eloquent and powerful address on the work of the Congre- gational Church Aid and Home blissicautry Society. The Society, he said, was an old one, dating back to the year" 1819, and from that time to this it had been seeking to pursue its . work. 'Sometimes hel was told that by seeking aid for that society he was injuring ;tile- ,Forelgn Missionary Society, but kis, , own aperience was just the opposite of that, for the man who gave for home missions was the very same man that would give for foreign missions, and the' man who gave for foreign missions was the very' same man who gave fot home missions. And he might say that they had not reached the point of Christian giving when the giving to one object meant the withholding from another. If they compared the givings of Christian people with their earning they would find it was a very small propor- that they gave to Christ as compared with what they used for themselves. He had been curious enough to analyse a list of givings by American Christians, and it came out like this. A man pro- fessing to be redeemed by Christ, and that he owed everything to Him, saved for himself .£lOO, and at the same time gave 1-16th of one per cent, for the conversion of the world to Christ—is 3d in the £lOO. Now, if the American Christians gave as liberally as the English Christians, and most people said they did, then they could see that the present rate of giving was out of all proportion with what God de- manded of them; and he was old-fashioned enough to believe that something of the depression that had been passing over their churches and over their country might after all be by reason of unfaithful- ness to that which was their duty, ' The withhold- ing from God what was due to him should result in God withholding from them what otherwise he would bestow upon them. Speaking of the general work of the societyhe represented, Mr. Mearns said that they aided in supplying to rural districts Evangelists who went from village to village preaching the Gospel. As an instance, he mentioned that in Berkshire one of their preachers had the care of a district containing six 'villages, in one of which he preached every sixth Sunday, and ar- ranged for lay preachers on other Sundays, while he also preached every night of the week in one or other of the villages. The society likewise aided ministers who had small churches, but this aid was given for mission work of an aggressive kind out- side the ministers ordinary sohere. The society did not confine its effortsto • rural districts, but also at- tended to the large centres of population. It would be a great mistake to suppose that rural districts deserved their care, but that they might neglect the large centres of population. At the same time they, must riot neglect the rural districts' for there was hardly a centre -in London Where the 'Christian workers had net ,been trained in village churches. These workers were doing a splendid service for the evangelisation of the large 'centres of ' population. In the yillages of Berkshire, a great number of agricultural labourers are out of work, and what were to 'become of of Evangelists receiving £6O, £7O, or £80? The labourers were now unable to give, and the incomes of, the Evangelists would be greatly reduced unless the society stepped into the broach. The labourers gave -what they could wen they had the means, but now they must look to some other country for a home. When they went away, however, they went as Christian men and women, and the result would , be that many a little Congregational Church would be formed in the coloniQs. That was the' way to evangelise the colonies. The special missions which had been in- stituted, by the society were next referred to. -The society was ,the first to instituteOpecial missidm to the -gips iles and the hop-pickers. He had recently been looking up some of tho Se. special Missions, aria hmong the hop-pickers he found that meetings of 'one kind or another had been carried on in the tents every night during the season. He chote the very last day of the season to go down, for the people received their money that day, and it used to be a day when there was no end of drinking:and .fighting. But on.the.day he went-down' he saw no drinking tO any extent; he
IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.

------ - A meeting of membprs of the Warrington branch of this league was held on Sunday afternoon in the League Hall, Warrington, the prinripat object of it being to hear an address by Mr. John O'Brien, of Liverpool, on the "Plan of campaign in Ireland." Mr. McLoughlin occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance of members. The Crummy, in opening the meeting, referred to the proposed testi- monial to Mr. T. P. O'Connor. They, he said, in common with other branches all over the country, must do some little towards it. No man in their party had done so much for the national cause in the United Kingdom as had Mr. I'. P. O'Connor. Were it not for him perhaps they would not be there that day, because it was to his indefatigable labours thht the splendid organisation . that now existed throughout tho country was due. Therefore he hoped they would do something towards the testimonial. tipeak- ing of the progress of the National League locally. the Chairman said that in Warrington they were growing in strength and numbers. The cause na- tionally Was also progressing, and they had great reason for congratulation. Every move that had been made, and many had been made of late, bad tended to strengthen their cause. Their opponents ' had within the last few months suffered many blows, and they had, after being in power only seven months, already begun to show the white feather. They must' not be surprised at what took place, but they must be prepared for anything that might turn up. Referring to the death of Lord Iddesleigh, he said that if ever ' man was treated meanly and contemptibly Lord Iddeeleigh was so treated, although no man served his -party so faithfully. „ He was an honourable opponent, and a man who always said what he thought, and let the way in which he would go' be understood.—Mr. Bran proposed, and Mr. P. O'Bauce seconded, the following resolution :—" Resolved that we Irishmen of War- rington here assembled desire to offer to the tenants of the Dillon estate our warmest congratulations on the grand victory they have achieved in the plan of cam- paign."—The resoltition was supported by Mr. JOHN O'Bantw (Liverpool), who referred at some length to the condition of Ireland. The official class in Ireland, he said, from the judges to those in the lowest grade, were drawn from the criminal—the landlord and aris'ocratic class. It was impossible for any honest 1 Irishman in Ireland, who did not belong to that criminal class, to get a position under Government. On the advice of Mr. Dillon, Mr. O'Brien, and other Irish leaders, the Irish peasantry had become united I and as one man. They were willing to give the land- lords a fair consideration for the use of the land, ac- cording to what amount of produce it yielded, but ' the landlords refused this, and the Plan of Campaign bad been put into operation in order to enable the Irish people to live in their own country. The land of any country was the property of the people—all had a stake in it—and it would be a bless- ing if some of those who kept up the land to them- selves would leave the country, even if they took their money with them. The Plan of Campaign was to en- able the people to live until there wasiin Dublin a Parlia- ment elected by the people, making laws for the I government of Ireland in accordance with the wishes ) and aspirations of her people. For the Irish farmers to form themselves into a great trade organisation was called immoral, even by English Liberals, bat there were several plans of campaign in England. There was a farmers' club' in Warrington, and last week the chairman, in proposing a resolution, said that if the landlords about Warrington did not reduce rents they would havetbe laud thrown on their hands, and would have to cultivateit as hese theycould. Did not that mean a plan of 'campaign ? The Plan of Compaign, he argued, was legal and moral. When Irishmen had their own Parliament and laws there would be no more law-abiding citizens than they. (Applause.)—The reso- lution baying been passed unanimously, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. O'Brien, and the motion of Mr. threareens, 'seconded by Mr. WHITBREAD, brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: WARRINCTON AND THE-QUEEN'S JUBILEE.
div.p: WARRINCTON AND THE-QUEEN'S JUBILEE.

Sir,—Sometime ago various ar.Pgestions were made as to how we should commemorate the Queen's .:übilee. Amongst others I noticed the Free Lending Library Scheme, put flrtls„ I understood, at the time. ands com- mittee was formed to considertLc same. May Ibe a:lowed to ask whether any progress has been made? What could he more acceptatle to the townspeople than a ;Free Lending LE)rary ? It would be a lasting sr ewcrial of the Queen's -jubilee affording a means of instruction and enjoyment to allwho chose to scull themselves of its-advan- tages. It would, moreover, be of great assistance to our boys to have the free use of books, and douttlase, many would avail thera-,elves of such a privilege who cannot do so under the present system. Cpportunities sadly wanting would thus be obtained. Against such institutions it is fre- quently argued that novel reading is promoted. Al:owing this to some extent, are not books so obtained of a higher and healthier tone than those too frequently read by the majority of our working people; while those who are not novel readers cir. obtain the ausistance they rece!re.— Yours, dm., L.R.

Sir,—Seeing there are various proposals as to whichAronld be the best way e: celebrating this year in Warrington, I .cannot help but suggest one for the benefit of the reeidents of this end of tbe town, namely; Eattersby-lane. and that is, that our Street Improvement Committee will make our so- called streets that ere may approach our homes with safety • and dry feet. &c. 'ln your issue of the 25th ult. I read a letter referring to The shugh of despond," by 'Anti Dirt." I quite erte..erse every word.he says, and mutt, repeat • the same complaint about our neighbourhood. I therefore think it would be -something for -us all to rejoice at if t aese abominable nuisances were swept ay.-ay du. ng 1887. 'Anti Dirt" is surprised that they have been r^sed from some epidemic breaking out. I regret to say we have not been so fortunate, as several persons have .been taken to the Fever Hospital, one case having proved fatal. If this ette of things is due to our landlords, wbere are our Medical Officer .of Health and Nuisance Inspector? Again, I suppose very shortly WC are Ito have a grand display at the °perks' of Hamilton-street new schools. I therefore trust an aproach to the same will be made worthy of the occasion; aisor the sake of the little ones that will have to attend it. .
Trusting some one will move at (tune in this matter for the benefit of us outside the centre of the town, I remaic, yourstAtsc.,

div.head: RATEPAYER.
div.p: A RATEPAYER.

Sir,—We are all waiting with great anxiety the result ef the contest in Liverpool 'between Mr. Neville and Mr. Gos- chen. On the issue widi depend, apart from the success of the Tory Government, which is now showing itself to he what its Irish name imptice "savage," whether, elated by success, we are to e invited by a Unionist (cc) Caucus. Already they are making their power over the purse felt in In many a division by withholding their assistance in the maintenance of organisation they helped to bring into ex- istence, while the rank and file look helplessly on, whereas by a little exertion they iniqtat easily help themselves, and dispense with this aid. Eat while so many valL.nt ones are to be found when their star is in the aseendant, how few there are to be seen when the political sky is overcast by a passing cloud, although we know perfectly well that the weather will clear up a,zain. After the winter of our die. content has passed away—then we shall hear the song birds again—and as sorrow and sighing, are by a wise proviso of nature soon forgotten, we shall bourgeon and grow like the palm tree, erect and stately; and to look at, not easily .cast down by a passing breeze, or even a hurricane eclipse of ,the sun. In plAin English, 1 fervently hope that Mr. Neville may win, and every tree Liberal should devontly wish he may.—Yours, &c.,
WAIT A LITTLE LONGER.

div.head: IMPRIMIS.
div.p: IMPRIMIS.

Sir,—When we were bov s together there need to be a popular song commencing "Cheer boys cheer "—what a hearty ring it had with it! I remember at that time, long ago it seems, that Mr. Russell used to electrify the people with the way he had of painting other and distant lands in bright colours. Your readers will remember the words of one song . . . .

- The world le wide. in lands beeidee There's rolm enouth for all. skipping from this song to another, we find the emigrant is supposed to have "wrought and strove from morn to night and saved his little store," Having accomplished this satisfactorily, he "sought his love" in England, and brought her o'er the sea— happy man. a happy wife, To bl. ss my home and me. Sir, lam led into this train of thought by no overwhelming wish to seek other lands. I think England beautiful, be- vond all comparison with other lands, but then you see— Men must work, and women must weep; There's little to earn, and many to keep, and thereby hangs a tate. If I was the Duke of Westminster, it is scarcely likely emigration would have come in my head, bat being poor' Colin Clout I find myself just a little bothered with things, and, Mr. Editor, I think you are a bit to blame for it. Look- ing through the "Examine-" I dropped en a paragraph about the Sankey Sugar works; 50 hands received notice to leave their employ, because of what? Weil, only because the em- ployers wanted to find Term for "a new and patent kind of machinery." Now, if 50 human beings bad had to leave their employ to find mom for machinery, I should have got into a rage, but as they were only "hands," well, it did'nt matter. I thought "serve 'em right; what right have hands' to cornp.te with machinery, let 'em starve, but leave us still our new machined." That last line, Mr. Editor, is some distance after Lord John Manners, eh ? But, sir, me and two or three tomilred friends of mine are getting just a little bit bothered with this new and parent machinery. The blessings we 3,9 receiving from it are so numerour, and come and go so quickly, that we are really unable to grasp them. The consequence is we altogether miss them, and are being left floundering in the ditches, where you will find us one of these days feeding on nettles, like the poor ,etches in Ireland. Mind you sir, I am not finding fault with machinery, be- cause I think it has brou4ht innumerable pleasures to some folks, if it has not brought increased happiness to us all. What matter ? But f..r it we should not have been able to feast the eye on the cu'side of all the beautiful mansions which stud our fair country sides. Excuse me, sir, I'll pull up; I was rushing into the poetic vein again, and what has poetry got to do with patent machinery. You see, Mr. Editor, it's when us rough, uncaltivated Chaps get down a bit, that we begin to study political econ- omy, and we do it in a fashion that is rather peculiar, We read that a demand always cinse+ a supply. Wall. if there has'nt been a demand fora hit of brass at our house durffig the last ten years it's a pity, I know the supply has been— nowhere. There, I must stop; that sort of talk, it's not nice, and it sounds so much like begging. Were you ever I at one of them meetings where they are supposed to relieve the poor, "the deserving poor," you know. Well, if you have been at such a meeting you must have heard some sleek; and well-starched gentleman or other,. express his

pleasure at the '.y pride and inderperlderrcecel th Eritieti workman, who wcruld rather starve at horne,rthan .parade his poverty abroad." I have heart: it -bftea. and 'have often noted the resifts, which are two-fold, bur-quite IorcaI: imposters only are poor, the rich refuse to help -nab, and they most piously button up their. pockets. The 'trump card you see, alt;-is always in the hands orthd deb. tlLet the poor wait for ' their chance. /X' yeti moor read "Billy'e rose ?" There is a line runs— " You must die tetra you're able, all these to enjoy." 11 There is another peosage occurs in a hook, -supposed to be greatly in favour erith the rich, which says -The first • shall be last, and the het first." What atleseed th:ng hope - is; there is a Danisiv proverb which says,"*lloper is an egg • of which one man gets the yolk, another the white. and a third the shell." Weil, I reckon we are haring the shell now ; the yolk will ccree ia "the Sweet try.rid•bye." I thought of telling you a bit about a-visit' ',paid to the • Public Hall when "ars deserving poor" were -having their tuck-out the otheYeay. It was a grim& sight for a man with a full etc mach to look upon. Kew the $d men did display their trainir.g in trencher ',ark'? '1 thanght some of the old men carried age well, but I won't mention that; the rich paid the piper. Anotber thing noticed was several men who could have bought and seld.plecety of the sub- scribers, but (Albeit Pll keep dark. Whattickled my fence: most was to see 'erne of my own shoomates trl cking it In; men working alosige.de me, and getting the same wage. Never mind, I theught it is easily understood, especially when you see tma parsons and .cirrares trotting up and down with the ale can and gill glans. .'alre thing would have been complete, I thought, if there bed been a Dis— senting parson or ri Catholic priest .present-but ne'er a one was bidden, I et:repose, so they staid away." 1' shouldn't like to see the old men's dinner t4one away with; but I should like to see them little lads and lasserrthat hawk sticks., kotber us about matches, and so onosittier down to a feast next Christmas. A chance this for the %Neocene., I think. But I'll stop, Mr. editor, or else I shall get serious. COLIN CLOUT.

That the inseention is sn ingenious one there is neoquestion, snd its very simplicity it 4 a saifidant proof of its value. • The directors are all practical men. and have taken up the 'mat- ter from a strictly business point of view.
