Library Committee oat of their difficulty. Some ' time ago their comnaitAke sent out circulars to all the subscribers of the library asking them a few questions and offering euggestions. Among the ! suggestions were that he present Library Commit- I tee should take as their line of• action the proposal to open. the lending depeetment of the library to , the public free of charge, on ' the understanding first that snliscriberteshanid have exclusive use, for twelve months, of the nee? •books purchased from the subscription, that I 1 the new books should afterwards be addled tottlei libraty ;and thirdly, that a special effort be made to increase the number of guinea subscribers; ' With, and lastly, that any deficiency ef funds or extra cost of carry- ing out the scheme 'be finally met, if I need be, by le-seeing a yebluntaty rate of led in the X. A voluntary rate for thevwould be required, and it would not be compulsory. The replies on the whole were very favourable to those questions; still they I were not suflicientlyees to -warrant them raising £l4O per annum—a BUM thatWOUld barely set the matter at rest. Ater that their committee thought fit to ap- point himself (Mr. Marrii) and Mr. John Roberts to see a few etentlemen, but they got no definite pro- mises. Through the ilifinence of their dear fnend Dr. Mackie, he was 'put in communication with a I prince among benefactors in the cause of education in this part of 'Lancashire, and the last letter he I received from that gentleman filled him with hopes that he vmuld freethat 'institution for them, and those hopee had nee yet died away, and somelday the oemmittee Who were- working with him might produce the needful amount, and make their library a free leading 'library. (Cheers.) He quoted the remarks of Professor :Huxley, that a most serious struggle for existence was approaching, and that struggle would -reflect most seriously on the pros- pects of the population of Lancashire and York- shire. These words he (Mr. Morris) said, appealed to every working-man and manufacturer. Last year he found that the St. Helens Free Lending Library issued 84,000 volumes, airainst 18,000 in the Warrington Library. 'He did not know the popula- tion of St. Rebus (Mr. Walker: 60,000.), but in Warriegton the 'population was about 50,000, so that they found that while 60,000 read 84,000 volumes, the TA6OO in Warrington read only 18,000 volumes. He thought that was a disgrace to them, for their youngenen were beaten about like a shut- tle cock, and aid 'not know where to spend their evenings, and •eould not go to the reading library because tthe place was filled. He would move "That this meeting of the burgesses and rate- payers of the borough of Warrington is strongly of opinion that it is desirable that the primary feature of the celebration of the Queen's Jubilee should be making the Warrington Library a Free Lending Library." (Cheers.) Mr. JOHN ROBERTS, in seconding the resolution, said he did so for the reason that by so doing they would be establishing a permanent benefit on them- selves as workingenen and on their children— (ap- plause)—and without doing an injustice to their employers. '(tffeer, hear.) He thought the free library was quite-necessary, and the sooner it was carried into operation the better. They had many working men and many of their children walking about the streets who would not think of going to the Library because it -was not a free lendingl library. He thought they, as working men, should have accommodation in the Library to take up a I book and remain and read it there if they desired, or to take the book home and read it. He did not know one reason why that could not be done. (Ap- plause.) He believed that at the present time the ratepaiers paid-one penny in the pound towardsthe expenses of this Library, which he thought brought in something like T.:580. That, in his opinion, was a good help towards making a free lending library. They did not want to raise the rates of Oh borough; as a committee they thought them already quite heavy enough. Ifthey looked at the question in a sensible way, they would see that they could not adopt any better insane to celebrate the Queen's Jubilee than by making the Library a free lending one. He hoped that they would conclude that that was the right coarse to adopt, and that they would do all that they could to carry out the movement. (Cheers.) Councillor Dixole supported the resolution. He felt, he said, very much interested in this question. Three or four years ago some people went to Ger- many from England, and one of them was brought into contact with an 'Englishman who had charge of a large engineering establishment. The traveller was much interested, and asked how it was that those who had served their apprenticeship in the foreign establishments were better scholars and could do their work at a lees cost than those in England could. The gentleman who had charge of the works leplied, "Our lads, when they enter on their apprenticeship, are required during the time of their apprenticeship to attend three, four, or five nights every week at some school after they have done their day's work." (Hear, hear.) The greatest difficulty that hp, as a member of the School Attendance Committee, had come across was that when children had passed the fifth, sixth, or seventh standards, a very small percentage of them found their way into the night schools. Where boys and girls took an interest in education, efforts should be made for them to have the opportunity of being further educated. Why should not they have a Free Lending Library, just the same as they had at other towns? They had many educational establishments at Warrington; and why not have this one? Ho*many of them would like to have books at home? Children, especially those who showed an aptitude, should have every facility fori advancing their education, and then they would be able to take many of the posts that were now filled by foreigners. To make the library a free lending one would be a boonp the town. (Cheers.) Mr. Jodie WALKER also supported the resolution. He was anticipating, he said, that there might be a little opposition to the free lending library question, or at any rate, that some ratepayers would make in- quiries. It was a matter about which he himself , had thought much, and he hoped that they would 1 consider all sides of the question. .With the rest, he very much deplored that Dr. Mackie, the mayor, could not , be present. Mr. Morris, himself, and some-others, saw Dr. 31ackie within three days of hisl lamentable breakdown in health, and had from him the strongest possible assurance that, so far as he was concerned as mayor, he woilld do all that he could to help the library question forward, and make it the primary feature of the Jubilee Year. :They felt that in the absence of the mayor that night, and perhaps throughout the year, they had lost a great supporter, but Dr. Mackie, as they would re- member, had in a letter placed before the Town Council his views upon the question of the Jubilee Year, and the first thing he mentioned in connec- tion with it was the possibility of making the library a'free lending library. (Applause.) That being the case he (the speaker) would sug- gest that it was, at any rate, In harmony with the views of the Mayor)hat they as rate- payers should, if they were in'agreement upon it, give-the matter their utmost support. Technically the chairman was right in saying that the library was 'free, but it did not go far enough. They re- cognised that at the present time they were paying ld in the pound, and some of them had been paying a library rate for thirty years. The full maximum that the law permitted had been paid, although they had only been receiving a minimum benefit. They in Warrington had a free library in so far that people could read hooks, free of charge, at the institution and in an excellent room. They hand an exeel- lent library, of some 20,000 volumes, a number very much beyond the average. They had an excellent museum—so excellent that he tbought they might for a time, at least, defer spending more money upon it—asid, having these things, he thought that now they saight go a step further, and lend out the books in the same way as was done in nearly every other town 'in the kingdom where there was a free library. (Cheers.) They had the books ready, and , it was simply a question of distribution. He had 1 yet to be persuaded that it would take much more money to conduct the institution as a free lending library than was already being spent upon it. Of course, with any public institution they could in- crease expenses year by year so long as money was supplied; they might spend £5O, £5OO, or £5,000. It was a question of cutting the coat according to the cloth, and if they made up their minds that the thing should be done, and in the Jubilee year— if the town set about it in a right spirit—in a very few months the library would be put on such a footing as would be a great benefit not only to the people themselves, but to their children's children. (Cheers.) It had been remarked that it was some- what pauperising to the people of Warrington that this thing should .be done. The answer to that Argument was simple. They as ratepayers con- tributed their £530 a year out of the penny rate, and were entitled eto the full value of what they contributed, !without there being the shadow of -pauperism about it. He would rather say that the pauperism, if there was any, was on the part of • those who, paying 5s a year only, took home the books that had, to a large extent, been purchased out of the 2500 given by the ratepayers. (Hear, I heee) Further, it bad been said that the books.

' would be:abused,Tand:vroirld netlike :et to put into decent people's hands. The answer to that also was simple. A hundred towns in the conntry had I already solved the problem, for they had.allowed ;their books to go free to the homes of people; and lit was a libel upon them to say that they abused the books. (Cheers.) Were they to be told that the ' people of Warrington were so snueli worse than the rest of the people of England, that they could not make a good use e the library? He declined to believe it. In Liverpool in 1883 nearly 400,000 volumes were lent out, and there was not, a single book lost to the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) Some few books, possibly, were lost, but their value was guaranteed by respectable house- holders, and nothing was lost to the rate- payers. He 'ventured to think that it would be the same in Warrington if the movement was car- ried out. (Cheers.) Mr. Morris had said that at St. Helens *boat 434,000 books were lent out, as against 18,000 in Warrington. That of itself was startling, hat in Warrington they had more books read in the reading-room, because they were not lent out free. There were 18,000 volumes lent out to subscribers, andsomething like 21,000 in addi- tion lent to people •whcovisited the reading-room. There were,tberefore, some 39,000 volumes issued during thwyearinithe two departments; but in-St. Helens theyhad 84,000 issued in the lending de- partmeirt, and some 4,000 in the reading-room—the reference department. That gave a total for *St. Helens of -88,000 as against 39,000 'for Warrington. (Hear, bear.) Now in Warrington, they had some 20,000 volumes as compared with 13,000 in St. Helens. In Wigan they issued three times as many booksasin 'Warrington. His mode of reasoning was that in Warrington the institution was only doing about one-third of its work. He thought that this 'was a stigma, some- thief; of .4 discredit to the town,. and • the best thing -they could do in the 'Jubilee Year was to take awaythe reproach. (Cheers.) It was simply a matter of economy on the past of the com- mittee to work with the penny rate if they could do nothing else. The sinking fund was lessening, they had the.building and books, and why, there- fore, should not the library be made a free lending library, as in other towns? With regard to the scheme Mr. Morris mentioned, he would say that it was inthe first' instance suggested by Mr. Robert Davies, a member of the Library Committee. He thought they-might begin first to lend the books out free. Then those who were subscribers, if could continue to subscribe on the under- istanduigthat they should have the control of the books they had bought for twelve months, tha books to be afterwards passed over to the Library Committee, so thitt the library would be always ensured a good supply of new books. When the matter came to be discussed, Mr. Davies, how- ever, concluded that that was a scheme that he could not sanction, as he found that there were difficulties about it. He (the speaker) believed that those in favour ofthe movement would not be sat- isfied until it was brought to a successful conclu- sion. (Cheers.) After they got a free lending library they would want a technical school— (cheers)—but one thing must follow another. The race was not always to the swift, nor the bat- tle to the 'strong; it was a matter now-a-days of knowledge, for knowledge was power, and as Shakesperebad said : Ignorance is the cures of God, """r`', Knowledge the wing wherewith we fly to heaven. (Cheers.) The Rev. E. C. E. Caurzercst expressed great sympathy with what had been said on behalf of the free lending library movement, and hoped that he should not be back- ward in assisting it to the best of his ability. The move- ment would be irresistible if demanded by the working people. Oa the Library Committee, they must kooc. were some gectlemen who were, perhaps, the best friends of edu- cation In the town, and he hoped that they would bear that in mind, and that they would give those gentlemen. though they might differ from them, the benefit of perfect honesty, and a desire likewise to further the interests of the working people in this matter. (Hear, bear.) The point with him was whether they should make a Jubilee question of it. He would rather have the question of a free library taken up Independently, as it was such a debatable one and might give rise a certain amount of strife. He believed that the friends of the movement would be able to carry it; but it was open to doubt whether it should be made a question of celebrating the Queen's Jubilee. (Applause.) Mr. H. WHITHAM, in supporting the resolution, said that he and a few more had been working on the library ques- tion, and had heard a considerable number of arguments used against it, but the objections made to it were not worthy of the acceptance of working men. A free library seemed to him to be the means O. enabling the rising generation to so improve themselves that they should be able to conmete with the foreigner. He was prepared to advise tits fellow working-men to go in for the movement thoroughly, and, if possible, bring it to a successful issue. (Cheers.) Why local magnates should go against it be could not understand, for their success in business depended greatly on their workmen being well educated and compe- tent. (Cheers.) The Rev. S. WILKINSON said that he approved of having the lending library free, but there were other things he would like to mention in connection with the jubilee year. He was told that baths had been suggested, and he really should like to see Warrington provided with better plunge baths, and also with Turkish baths. (Cheers.) Allusion was also made to an exhibition of local manufactures, but be did not know whether it would be approved, because be believed that in Liverpool the exhibition had not been a perfect success. He for one should be glad to see the li- brary free, but there was one thing that he wished to men- tion. That was the need of a church for St. Peter's parish. , (Cheers.) Mr. GEO. WOODS thought that if an exhibition was held, I it would, under the cireumstancee, turn out to be a thorough farce, and an utter failure. He thought, however, that there would be some sense in making the lending library free. If the weirking-men of Warrington united and were determined in their efforts they would have a free lending library. (Cheers.) The DEPUTY MAYOR observed that he thought it was only fair that inasmuch as there did appear to be another question to be discussed they should hear it discussed before they voted. As no gentleman rose to speak, the Deputy Mayor, after a pause, said be could not permit same of the remarks of the previous speakers to pass unchallenged. He Woes friend to the establishment of a free library, and would willingly subscribe towards the establishment of an institution of that kind. (Applause.) He wished to make a few remarks in justice to his native town of Warrington. If he did not, anyone reading the remarks made that night would think that Warrington was hostile to the advance- ment of education. He thought that was effectually dis- pelled by the simple fact that Warrington, up to the pre- Rent, bad been able to resist all the attempts of those who had advocated the establishmen't of a School Board, and that was strong proof that Warrington had not neglected education, but had done everything it could for the promotion of education, and consequently the promotion of the welfare of . its people. (Applause.) In contrasting the number of books issued at St. Helens Free Library with the number issued at Warrington, he said they ought to know what kind of books were issued at St. Helens. He added that if they starved their museum or art gallery in order to increase the Lomita in the library and ill order to make it free, he thought it would be a very doubtful- advantage. He urged they could not make the library free under the present circumstances, although there was no hostility on the part of the Library Committee or Tone Council to interpose any obstacle to the promotion of the free library. Mr. Unswonam said he was in no way opposed to the scheme that had been suggested that evening, bat be pro- posed they should have an exhibition of local manu- factures and tradesmen's productions in the Drill Hall, which he thought could be got up at little expense, and it would attract many people to Warrington. His proposition was "That the year of Jubilee be celebrated by holding an ex- hibition of local industries, where practical,. and that the Town Council be requested to give its *sanction and sup- port." (Applause.) The speaker at some length declared his experience of exhibitions, and urged that as Warring- ton was a town of varied industries they might have a very successful exhibition. After a pause, Mr. A. RATHBONE formally seconded the proposition. Mr. KNEEN Said he had been connected with similar exhibitions elsewhere, and he thought if they worked unitedly it could be brought to a successful issue. (Hear, \ hear) I Following a few remarks from the Depute Mayer, Mr. ' llratirEtt said that with regard to the exhibition, unless they were sure that the local manulacterers were prepared to give it their support it woad be a failure. He had spokientoeevienrsatal instance he thingrgtemanufacturers upon the question and n every was " pooh-poohed." They said that even if it could be done, and they believed it could, the present was not the time, and that as they were going to have two big exhibitions within 20 minutes' run from 1 Warrington, they could not expect to attract many people to Warrington. Mr. T. Heacnaer. commented on the expense that an ex- hibition of local manufactures would entail nn the producers I of heavy goods, and remarked that he did not think it would be worth their while at the present time to enter into such a i project, Mr. Evans asked if they were to ucderstand that the ex- tra cost would be £l3O per annum if the library was ' made free, and if the £7,000 mentioned by the Deputy- Mayor was a sinking fund to raise the money. The CHAIRMAN said that he was told that it would in- volve the necessity of raising something like that sum. Mr. WATERT& said that the necessity of raising £7,000 was a matter of opinion. It would be better to have the money, but if a penny could not be raised, and the cora- mines set themselves resolutely to the task, they could do it with the present income. The CHAIRMAN said that the Library and Museum had already incurred a debt of £5OO or £OOO. Mr. W. Rooms remarked that there were several ways In which the revenue might be increased, and asked why

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OCR (MN CORRYSFONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. Business on the Stock Exchange during the past week has been reduced to a minimum. The public bold aloof to 'such an extent that brokers are loud in their expressiona of something more than sor.ew, and are reduced to " swopping coats" among theraeelvc, a to result being that prices all round droop from the a'm ice of any support. The decla- ration of dividends on the part t f railway companies and banking firms is the one redeeming feature of- the week, as in the majority of cases an provement on the correspondieg period of the previous year is shown.. An attempt is being made in same quarters to explain away any im- provement shown by drawing attentioe to the fact that, as far as railways are concerned, the improved dividenda ace due entirely to reduction of working expenses. This may be applicable to one or two lines, but in the majority of cases there can be no doubt that to the ancmented trade is due the increase in the dividends. The Southern lines, which have more especially declared better dividends, the Increased traffic returns alone are suScient to account for the increase, and the natural inference is that people have had more money to spend on pleasure. The Nor- thern lines are dependent more especially open goods ,rafile, and cannot fail to be a barome- trical indicator of the more important productions of the coantry, but against this point it must ba borne in mind that the competition is all the more severe which en- courages some companies to work at a lose for a time in the hope of securing ultimate profits. Holders of Bryant and May should realiee at present prices as, apart from the in- liition imparted 'o them there is a heavy Parcel of thosa shares which will be thrown on the market at the first convenient opportunity, and cannot fail to depress prices. Promoters are beginning to move now and two gold mines have already been offered the public. The only industrial company, however, is the Union Boot and Shoe Machine Company, Limited, with a capital of £50,000, which has been formed for the purpose of acquiring, Ideveloping, and working the patents, rights, and inventions for the United Kingdom in certain fastening and wire- making machines for uniting the soles and uppers of boots and shoes. The chief feature of the.patent is its time and , lahcnr-saving process, one man being able to complete 5001

With all due respect to the Deputy Mayor, he would 'very much have preferred that the Kayor was in his place that night, for without a doubt their cause was suf- fering through his absEnce. Their desire was that the usefulness of that institution might be in- creased, that men who had no books at home might go there any evening and have g rest and read, and 19othat those who Pocked to the library might be able to take boeks home, so as to make room for those who wantea to make use of the reference room. A few nights so, he was told that one man went into the reading room and could not find a place to sit down. He had been toiling hard all day, and when he got to the reading room he found it was crammed by youths from the various schools preparing for examinations. To make the library into a free lending one, one of three eourses must be taken. Either the committee that man- aged the institution must have an extra farthing added to the penny rate; or the expenses of the institution must be reduced, or some generous gen- tleman or gentlemen must come to their assistance. The first of the three, he understood, the Corpora- tion were dead set against it, and, although there were many workmen in favour of the rate being raised, and several people had urged him to go in favour of it, he must candidly confess it found no favour with him. The rates were now high enough in this town. (Cheers.) As regards the second suggestion, he could not say anything definite, as he had never gone into the question. There were some people who condemned the committee for ex- travagance and inconsistencies, but he expected if that Library Committee, or any other Library C3mmittee, were composed of angels from heaven, there would be found someone that I could or would put a black mark against them, and therefore that matter he would leave for further investigation. div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
A reward 0f.550 has been offered for the identification of 'the person who gave the alarm of fire at the Hebrew Dra- matic 'Club• which resulted in the loss of 17 lives. _ _
DEATH OF LORD CHESTERFIELD.—The Earl of Chester- field, of Holm Lacy, Hereford, died on Friday morning at St. Leonards-on.Sea. His lordship was born in 1821, and is succeeded by Lead Stanhope.

• NEW LIBRARY FOR notTox.—The Library Committee of the Bolton Corporation have resolved to open a jubilee branch library. on land presented by Mr. John Heywood, M.A., J.P. This will make the third branch library in the town.

_ FIRE AT A PRINTING WORES.—On Friday morning the 6' Guardian" printing works at Jarrow were burned to the ground, and the contents almost entirely destroyed. 'The amount of damage will be considerable. The CALM of the outbreak is not yet ascertained,

BRITISH AwsrixerioN.—Friday night's Gazette "states that the Queen hay been pleased to grant letters patent to be pressed under the great seal of the United Kingdom for the annexation of certain islands, known as the Kermadec group, to the colony of New Zealand. CONFERENCE OF LIBERAL LEADERS. - Nearly all the members of the late Cabinet have made arrangements to come to London next Monday, the same day as Mr. Glad- stone; and there will probably be a consultation between them on Tuesday at Carlton House-terrace, where Mr. Glad- stone will reside.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT CHESTER STATION.—On Friday morning, about ten o'clock, a shocking railway accident occurred at Chester General Railway Station to a man named Edward Jones, employed as a brake examiner. From the particulars, it appears he was discovered lying on the back line in the centre of the station, with his head smashed in a frightful manner. An inquest will be held. FIRE NEAR DEWSIDIRY.-00 Friday, a fire broke out in the waste pulling room of a large new mill belonging to Messrs. Day, Chadwick, and Co., wool and waste dealers, Batley Carr, near Dewsbury, and before the flames could be extinguished the building was gutted. Three fire brigades were playing on the flames up to eleven o'clock. The damages are exceedingly heavy. The loss is fully in- sured.

_ _ Tam Hountrrow COLLIERY DISASTER.—At Barnsley Police Court, on Friday, the enginernan, Allen Beresford, the hanksman, and Albert Holdsworth were charged with the manslaughter of the ten man who were killed at Houghton main colliery on December 30th. The men lost their lives through the over draught of the cage, and the accus.d were on duty at the time. The magistrates held that there was no case against Holdsworth, and he was dis- charged, but they intimated their intention of committing Beresford for trial.

BCESE AT A Cams Tau FUNERAL.—An extraordinary scene occurred at a feneral in Chester on Friday afternoon. A man named John Candeland died, and the funeral arrange- ments .Tere made for Friday afternoon, when the usual vehicles for the conveyance of the corpse and the friends to the burial around, as well as a number of Oddfellows, met at the house. To the astonishment of the undertaker and friends, all the doors of the house were found fastened, it is stated, by the neighbours, who demanded payment for at- tention to the deceased in his illness. The friends of the deceased were ultimately compelled to burst the doors open in order to abtain the corpse, and after much delay the cortege proceeded to the cemetery, where the corpse was buried.

A TERRIBLE STRUGGLE. On Friday morning a fearful scene was enacted in Birmingham. A man named Lascelles returned to his wife after an ab- sence of seven years, and declared he would kill ner. He pulled out a sharp knife and turned the gas out. The terrified woman ran into a neighbour's house, and the police were sent for. A police officer arrived at a forunate moment, and saved the woman. The man threatened to cut his own throat if the police touched him. The officer made a dash at him, whereupon the would-be murderer backed away at his throat. The policeman chased him round the table, the desperate fellow sawing away at his throat all the time, till he fell down exhausted from loss of blood. He now lies at the hospital.

div.head: MR. STANLEY'S DEPARTURE.
div.p: MR. STANLEY'S DEPARTURE.

Mr. H. M. Stanley left Charing Cross at eight o'clock on Friday night with the Indian mail train, via Brindisi. The British India steamship with the baggage belonging to the expedition sailed on Thursday. Mr. Stanley, who was in splendid spirits, was loudly cheered. LOSS OF A STEAMER AND 15 LIVES.

- A Stornoway correspondent telegraphs on Friday after- noon that telegraphic communication between Stornoway and Dist, which has been interrupted for a considerable time, was restored on Friday, and we now learn that the Norwegian steamer Defiance, of Bergen, ran ashore last Monday night, South of 11ishinist light, in S nith Uist. Four bodies have been washed ashore, and there can be no doubt that the whole crew, to the number of abmlt 15, have been lost. When srat seen the steamer's how was out of the water, whilst her stern was submerged thirty feet, but she has since broken up and sunk. The D- ti ince was seven hundred tons gross, and was owned by Hilelvorsen and Co., Bergen. She left Liverpool last Saturday in behest for Blyth, there to load coal for Bergen, and also to be over- hauled preparatory to returning to Liverpool next March.

PARIS, FRIDAY EVF.NING.—The Budget Committee has rejected the Government financial schemes, and another Ministerial crisis is tberefoae feared. A WAR VESSEL SUNK. —EIGHTY MEN MISSING.

SITANGHAI, FRIDAY.—The Peninsular and Oriental Com- pany:a steamer Nepaul came into collision on Friday with a Chinese war vessel at the entrance of the Wtiangpo. The Chinese vessel sank, and eighty of her crew are reporteu to be missing. No one was hurt on board the Nepaul,

' The invention is an American one. and the vendor has se- cured the patent rights for the United Kingdom. The process has already been adopted by the largest manufacturers in America, and several million pairs of boots and shoes have been made under the invention. The reports which have ' been received from the trade speak Of the merits of the fas- tening in the highest terms. The vendor states, and is con- firmed in his representation by she Secretary of the Union Metallic Fastening Company of America, who are manufac- turers of the machines made according to the said Invention, that there are now in use in that country over 80 machines. The fastening has in itself many important and striking features which command the attention, not only of the trade. but also of the genecal public. It is economical in working, and simple in operation. As a proof of the striking success obtained by the machine attention is drawn to the testimorrals which accompany the prospectus from the following leading manufacturers, viz. : Stowe. Bills, and Hawley, Potter, White. and Bayley. A. P. Martin, and Co., Houghton, Coolidge, and Co.,John O'Connell and Sons, Leighton Brothers, William Chain Coborn and Co., H. H. Mawhinny, and Co. Pocock Brrthers, A. and W. Flatau and Co.. As. ; and subscriber: are also referred to the extracts from the press which accompany the prospt ctus. The earning capacity of one fastening machine to the Com- pany by its consumption of the patent wire is 25s per diem, so that it would onlyrequire a sale or in Ise of 30 machines to earn a dividend of 22i per cent per annum on the capital of the Company. There are in Great Britain over 500 manufacturers of boots and shoes, the output being something like 130,000,000 pairs per annum. It will thus be seen that the demand for the new process pos,essing such great merits will be very large; it is not, however, expected that the existing mode of fastening the soles of boots and shoes will be immedi- ately revolutionhed, but it is fair to suppose that this process will come into general use, and it is estimated that at least 30 machines can be placed within the first twelve months. This cannot be considered other than a very moderate estimate, inasmuch as over 80 machines have been placed in America during the first two years of its introduction there. The machines have already been adopted by the following English firms:—Stead, Simpson, anti Nephews, A. and W. Platen and Co.. William Hickson and Sons, Pocock Brothers, and Freeman, Hardy, and Willis, Limited. The validity of the patents has been satisfactorily reported upon by Messrs. Haseltine, Lake. and Co., the well-known patent agents, and the vendor has in consequence warranted the validity of the patents. The only contracts entered into are as follow—namely, one dated the 18th January, 1887. between Edward Baylies Seaver. the vendor, at the ore part, and the Company of the other part; and another dated the 3rd day ot January, 1817, between the said Edward 1..ta3 lies Beaver and the General Assets Pur- chase Company, Li,dited. The price to be paid for the patent is £40,000 in cash. The balance of capital—viz., £lO,OOO- the Directors consider ample for working the business. Owing to the regulations of the London Stock Exchange the vendor cannot contract ro take any portion of the purchase mousy In shares without precluding the Company from obtaining an official quotation. He has, however, already applied as one of the public for nineteen thousand four hun- dred sharea. In cases where no allotments are made all moneys paid by shareholders will be returned in full. The contracts and reports of Messrs. Haseltize, Lake, and Co. can be seen at the offices of the a 'Bettors of the Com- pany. Prospectuses and forms of application can Ye obtained at the offices of the Company, and of the Bankers, Prtkers, and Solicitors.
